Stay up to date with AI tools, model releases, and developer workflows that matter.

Prompt caching reduces LLM token costs by reusing a previously processed prompt prefix so the provider skips the need to re-tokenize and re-encode it on subsequent requests. This tutorial walks through building a TypeScript request-builder and usage-logging helper that normalizes prompt caching behavior across all three providers in Node.js.

Prompt caching reduces LLM token costs by reusing a previously processed prompt prefix so the provider skips the need to re-tokenize and re-encode it on subsequent requests. For Node.js developers making repeated API calls with stable system instructions, few-shot examples, or long reference documents, prompt caching can deliver up to 90% cost reduction on cached tokens.

The problem is that three major providers — OpenAI, Anthropic, and Gemini — each implement prompt caching differently. Opt-in mechanisms, minimum token thresholds, TTL behavior, cache-hit indicators, and discount rates all vary. Developers must piece together incompatible documentation.

The result is a single factory function that constructs cache-optimized requests and a unified logger that verifies cache hits regardless of provider.

This tutorial walks through building a TypeScript request-builder and usage-logging helper that normalizes prompt caching behavior across all three providers in Node.js. The result is a single factory function that constructs cache-optimized requests and a unified logger that verifies cache hits regardless of provider.

Prerequisites: Node.js 20+, TypeScript 5+, an API key for at least one of the three providers, and familiarity with async/await and REST API consumption.

All three providers cache from the beginning of the prompt forward — only the prefix qualifies. A "stable prefix" is any content that does not change between requests: system instructions, few-shot examples, long reference documents, or boilerplate context. Keep the prefix byte-identical across calls. Any mutation, even a whitespace change, invalidates the cache and forces a full re-processing pass.

Prompt design matters. Front-load all static content and append variable content (the user's actual question, dynamic context) at the end.

The following table captures the critical differences across OpenAI, Anthropic, and Gemini:

For explicit caching, Gemini requires the largest minimum prefix at 32,768 tokens, making it suitable only for very large context windows. Gemini 2.5 and newer also enable implicit caching by default, which works more like OpenAI’s automatic approach. Anthropic offers the steepest read-token discount at 90%, though Anthropic bills cache creation calls at 25% above standard input pricing. OpenAI is zero-config but offers the smallest discount at 50%.

Update tsconfig.json with these essentials:

The CacheAwareRequest holds the provider-agnostic input shape. The CacheUsageReport normalizes the output so that calling code never needs to know which provider-specific field indicates a cache hit. The cachedTokenDiscountPercent reflects the provider's discount rate on cached tokens, while estimatedCostSavingsPercent approximates actual savings relative to total tokens.

OpenAI caches automatically. There is no flag to set, no resource to create. The only requirement is that the prompt prefix must be at least 1,024 tokens long. The system message is the natural place for the stable prefix.

The systemPrompt string should contain the full stable prefix. As long as it exceeds 1,024 tokens and remains identical across calls, OpenAI will cache it automatically within its TTL window.

Anthropic requires explicit opt-in via a cache_control breakpoint. The breakpoint is placed on the last content block of the stable prefix. Everything before (and including) that block is cached; everything after is processed fresh.

The cache_control: { type: "ephemeral" } annotation marks the boundary. On the first call, Anthropic reports cache_creation_input_tokens. On subsequent calls within the 5-minute TTL, it reports cache_read_input_tokens instead.

Gemini uses a two-step process. First, create a cachedContent resource via a separate API call, specifying the content and an explicit TTL. Then reference that resource in subsequent generateContent calls. The minimum prefix is 32,768 tokens.

Note: The GoogleAICacheManager class may be exported from @google/generative-ai/server rather than the top-level @google/generative-ai depending on your installed SDK version. If the import below fails, try import { GoogleAICacheManager } from "@google/generative-ai/server". Verify with: node -e "const m = require('@google/generative-ai'); console.log(typeof m.GoogleAICacheManager)" — if it prints undefined, use the /server subpath.

The cached content object must be stored and reused. If the TTL expires, the resource must be recreated. In production, persist the cached content name to a database or cache store to survive process restarts; the in-memory Map used in the factory below is lost on every cold start, causing redundant cachedContent creation and additional billing.

A single factory function dispatches to the correct provider-specific builder and returns a normalized shape alongside the raw response for usage inspection.

A single factory function dispatches to the correct provider-specific builder and returns a normalized shape alongside the raw response for usage inspection.

The Gemini path stores cached content objects in a Map keyed by a SHA-256 hash of the full system prompt, avoiding both redundant cache creation on repeated calls and cache key collisions that could occur with prefix-based keys. A secondary inflight Map ensures that concurrent requests with the same prompt do not trigger duplicate cache creation calls.

OpenAI exposes cache data at response.usage.prompt_tokens_details.cached_tokens. When this value exceeds zero, the request hit the cache.

Anthropic splits caching into two fields: response.usage.cache_creation_input_tokens (populated on the first request when the provider writes the cache) and response.usage.cache_read_input_tokens (populated on subsequent requests that read from it). Check whether cache_read_input_tokens > 0 to confirm a hit.

Check response.usageMetadata.cachedContentTokenCount. If it exceeds zero, the cached content resource was used for that request.

The cachedTokenDiscountPercent reflects the provider's discount rate applied to cached tokens specifically. The estimatedCostSavingsPercent approximates the actual savings relative to total tokens in the request — for example, if only 100 of 10,000 tokens were cached at Anthropic's 90% rate, the estimated savings would be ~0.9%, not 90%. The hash comparison across requests reveals whether the prefix changed. The token estimate uses a 1.3x multiplier on word count as a rough approximation (+-30% error); production systems should use provider-specific tokenizers (e.g., tiktoken for OpenAI) for precision.

Cache misses happen for several concrete reasons. You changed the prefix between requests (even whitespace or trailing newline differences count). Your prefix falls below the provider's minimum token threshold. The TTL expired — Anthropic's 5-minute default is particularly aggressive. You switched the model parameter between requests. Or, in Gemini's case, you did not pass the cachedContent name to the generation call.

Run with npx tsc && node dist/demo.js openai. Swap the argument to anthropic or gemini to test other providers. The first request populates the cache; the second reads from it.

Realistic savings depend on reuse frequency within the TTL window. OpenAI provides a 50% discount on cached input tokens. Anthropic provides 90% on cached read tokens, though Anthropic bills cache creation calls at 25% above standard input pricing. Gemini provides 75% for Gemini 1.5 Pro (the Flash rate is not confirmed at time of writing). Anthropic reports reduced latency on cache hits, but none of the three providers publish fixed latency benchmarks for caching; consult each provider's official prompt caching documentation for current figures.

These savings only materialize when the same prefix is reused frequently within the cache's TTL. A prefix that changes on every request, or one that falls below the provider's minimum token threshold, will never trigger caching, and you will pay standard pricing.

Start by adding streaming response support to the request-builder, since cached prefixes work with streaming on all three providers. From there, implement persistent TTL management for Gemini's cachedContent resources (which otherwise require manual recreation after expiry), and wire the cache usage logger into an observability pipeline like OpenTelemetry spans for production cost monitoring.

For full details on each provider's caching behavior, consult the official documentation: OpenAI Prompt Caching, Anthropic Prompt Caching, and Gemini Context Caching.

#10652. Scientists turn DNA into a memory device that uses 100x less power

DNA serves as the genetic blueprint for every living organism, but it is also an extraordinarily dense way to store information. A single gram can hold about 215 million gigabytes of data. Bringing that remarkable storage capacity into electronics could lead to more efficient data centers, faster processing and systems capable of handling increasingly complex information.

The challenge has been finding a way to make biological DNA function effectively alongside electronic materials. Penn State researchers have now developed an approach designed to overcome that incompatibility.

The work, published in Advanced Functional Materials and the subject of a patent application, relies on two key components. One is synthetic DNA, made from commercially available, chemically engineered molecules arranged into short genetic sequences tailored for specific electronic requirements. The other is crystalline perovskite, a semiconductor already used in technologies including solar cells, lasers and data storage devices.

"Biology and electronics are different domains," said Kavya S. Keremane, co-corresponding author and postdoctoral researcher in materials science and engineering at Penn State. "Bridging these two fields required developing an entirely new materials platform that allows them to function seamlessly together. By combining the information storage capabilities of DNA with the exceptional electronic properties of perovskite semiconductors, we created a bio-hybrid system that fundamentally changes how low-power memory devices can be designed."

Using these materials, the team created a memory resistor, known as a "memristor," that operates with very little energy. Unlike ordinary resistors, which maintain a set resistance to electrical current in devices ranging from cell phones to space shuttles and lose their stored information when power disappears, memristors can preserve a record of previous electrical activity. They can remember the direction in which current previously flowed even after the power source is removed.

That ability allows information to be stored and processed in the same place, resembling the way neurons function in the brain. Such an arrangement could support more simultaneous and sophisticated forms of data processing. According to the researchers, however, practical commercial systems would still require enough storage capacity and electrical power to become costly and inefficient without DNA's ability to pack enormous amounts of information into a very small space while consuming little energy.

"As the demand for artificial intelligence (AI) grows, we need a new strategy for low-power, high-storage devices," said Bed Poudel, co-corresponding author and research professor of materials science and engineering at Penn State.

Poudel said AI and other emerging technologies are expected to depend increasingly on neuromorphic computing, which is designed to operate more like the human brain. Such systems can evaluate multiple inputs at once while making decisions informed by previous experiences and future priorities.

"Usually, it takes more power to store more information. Our device, however, consumes 100 times less power and the storage capacity is higher than traditional storage devices, like flash drives."

To construct the device, the researchers added silver nanoparticles to a layer of customized DNA sequences -- specially designed to be of certain compositions and lengths -- that was integrated with thin films of perovskite.

This technique, called "doping," involves introducing a small amount of another material to produce specific properties. In this case, adding the silver nanoparticles allowed the DNA to conduct electricity while also helping its molecular units line up in a more orderly arrangement.

Synthetic DNA offered another important advantage over natural DNA. Unlike natural DNA -- long, entangled strands that behave like wet spaghetti when handled -- short and rigid pieces of synthetic DNA can be arranged with much greater precision at extremely small scales.

According to co-author Neela H. Yennawar, research professor and director of the Penn State Huck Institutes of the Life Sciences' Biomolecular Interactions Core Facility, molecularly engineered DNA can provide structural organization, adjustable electrical conductivity and functional control that natural DNA cannot achieve when incorporated into thin films.

"We can computationally determine exactly which sequences we need and how long they should be, and then we can rationally design them with synthetic DNA," Yennawar said. "These structures can be systematically doped with silver and other ions and engineered to interface seamlessly with perovskites -- transforming DNA from a biological macromolecule into a programmable, multifunctional nanomaterials platform."

When combined, the silver-doped DNA and perovskite formed bio-hybrid pathways that directed the flow of electrical current through the device.

The researchers found that electrons moved reliably when they applied less than 0.1 volt -- for comparison, standard U.S. outlets have 120 volts -- and the device responded predictably when the direction of the current was changed.

The carefully designed DNA structures, combined with the perovskite, also helped make the device unusually stable. According to the team, it continued operating consistently at temperatures approaching 250 degrees Fahrenheit and remained functional at room temperature for more than six weeks, substantially exceeding the performance standards of existing perovskite-based memory storage devices.

The researchers also reported that the new system could perform the same memory function as comparable technologies while consuming only one-tenth as much power. That level of efficiency could make the approach especially attractive for future electronics designed to handle large amounts of information with lower energy demands.

"Using just the DNA or just perovskite alone did not produce near as robust a result as the combination," Keremane said. "It's this combination that enables a very high memory storage density that requires very little power."

A New Direction for Bio-Inspired Electronics

The team now plans to improve the technology further and explore additional uses for bio-inspired electronic systems.

"Nature has the solution -- we just have to find it and apply it," Poudel said. "This work of integrating DNA into electronics to do amazing things gives a glimpse into what is possible."

In addition to Keremane, Yennawar and Poudel, other Penn State co-authors include co-corresponding author Luyao Zheng, postdoctoral research in materials science and engineering; Haodong Wu, doctoral student in materials science and engineering; Jiamao Zheng, who was a master's student in materials science and engineering at the time of research and has since graduated from Penn State; Shashank Priya, who was a professor of materials science and engineering at the time of research; and Chiranth C. Ravi, who was a master's student in the Huck Institutes of the Life Sciences at the time of research and has since graduated from Penn State. Abhinav Gorthy and co-corresponding author Rashmi Jha, chemical engineering and materials science, University of Minnesota, also contributed.

The U.S. National Science Foundation, the National Institutes of Health, Penn State and the University of Minnesota supported this research.

Materials provided by Penn State. Note: Content may be edited for style and length.

#10651. Electric hypercar wrecks at 280 mph during test, driver returns for even faster run

A nearly 3,000-horsepower electric hypercar crashed during a high-speed test while attempting to reach 280 mph, but its driver escaped without serious injuries before the manufacturer returned for an even faster run.

Chinese automaker BYD shared footage of its Yangwang U9 Xtreme crashing into a guardrail during testing, leaving much of the vehicle destroyed while its carbon-fiber cabin remained intact.

The incident comes as BYD prepares to push the electric hypercar beyond its previous top speed of 308 mph, with the company targeting a new record of more than 310 mph.

According to Electrek, the Yangwang U9 Xtreme was undergoing a series of high-speed tests when the accident occurred.

During its first run, the vehicle exceeded 217 mph before reaching more than 261 mph on its second attempt. The third run was intended to push the car beyond 280 mph, but it ended when the hypercar lost control and slammed into a guardrail.

Footage shared by BYD shows the vehicle striking the barrier before spinning across the track, with debris scattering across the road. The front and rear sections sustained extensive damage, although the central carbon-fiber passenger compartment remained intact.

Despite the crash, the driver escaped without serious injuries. BYD confirmed that the driver underwent a comprehensive medical examination at a hospital, where doctors determined they were in good health.

The manufacturer subsequently resumed testing, with another run reaching 284.5 mph, exceeding the speed targeted during the earlier crash. Yangwang representative Jiang Gong said there was still room for improvement and expressed confidence that the vehicle could eventually surpass 310 mph.

The Yangwang U9 Xtreme is powered by four electric motors producing nearly 3,000 horsepower. It also features a 1,200-volt electrical system and motors capable of reaching 30,000 rpm.

Electric hypercar sets new top speed record with 308.4 mph run

New Chinese bullet train shatters world record by going 497 mph in 5.3 seconds

Chinese ‘Superman’ robot beats Usain Bolt’s top speed – before crashing into a wall

In September 2025, the hypercar reached 308.3 mph during testing in Germany, establishing a new benchmark for production-car top speed.

BYD is now preparing another attempt to exceed 310 mph, with Dubai previously identified as the planned location for a record run in November 2026. However, the company has not confirmed a final date for the attempt.

The automaker ended its crash footage with a message indicating that it intends to continue pursuing higher speeds.

“The ultimate pursuit has no end; the summit will eventually be reached,” BYD said in a statement translated by Electrek.

#10649. Microsoft Links Storm-0940 to ConnectWise Supply Chain Attack

The China-linked actor used an AI-enabled penetration-testing tool to automate and accelerate its attack on more than 2,200 tenants.

A China-linked threat actor that Microsoft tracks as Storm-0940 used an agentic AI penetration-testing framework to accelerate a supply chain attack involving ConnectWise Cloud Backup.

The attackers used compromised application credentials associated with the service to attempt to access the Microsoft 365 environments of more than 2,250 downstream customer tenants. In multiple instances, the attackers obtained privileged access to an organization’s cloud infrastructure in less than three hours after initial targeting, Microsoft said in an analysis published this week.

The activity demonstrates how threat actors are integrating agentic AI into existing offensive security workflows and scaling their operations exponentially, Microsoft researchers wrote. "While the majority of the targeting wasn't successful, Storm-0940 achieved privileged cloud persistence at many organizations in a brief time," they said.

Related:Philippine Migrant Worker Data Likely Leaked in 69GB Government Breach

ConnectWise provides software and IT management technology that managed service providers use to deliver a broad range of services to their customers, including backup and recovery for Microsoft 365 data. Delivering these services requires the company to have authorized application access to customer Microsoft 365 environments to back up and restore data.

On Oct. 16, ConnectWise disclosed unauthorized access to application identities associated with its Cloud Backup product. The company subsequently published additional details and containment guidance but has not publicly explained how the attackers initially gained control of the application identities.

Microsoft described the incident as part of a broader Storm-0940 campaign that began as early as September and targeted hundreds of organizations worldwide across several industries including manufacturing, aerospace, chemicals, energy, defense, and financial services. The threat actor has been using an AI penetration-testing framework called ARTEX to automate and accelerate its operations.

"In multiple affected environments, Microsoft observed AI-accelerated follow-on activity through Microsoft Graph, including reconnaissance, application credential changes, and attempts to modify privileges that could enable expanded or persistent access," Microsoft said.

In the ConnectWise incident, Storm-0940 used ARTEX to accelerate reconnaissance and scanning, password spraying, and OAuth application abuse. The threat actor used ARTEX to attempt sign-ins to more than 2,250 tenants, generating as many as 2,900 sign-in attempts per minute. That pace left defenders with little time to detect and respond to the activity, Microsoft noted.

Related:One Compromised Laptop, Billions Lost: The Binance Attack-Path Warning

"Storm-0940's activity illustrates how a threat actor with a broad target set can use an agentic AI tool and privileged authentication material to quickly attempt to compromise many organizations," the company said.

ConnectWise suspended its Cloud Backup service and also took its SaaS Security and Cloud Management services offline following the incident. In an Oct. 22 update, the company noted it was continuing work on restoring disrupted services and urged customers to keep affected ConnectWise application connections offline until further notice.

"Investigation and monitoring continue alongside restoration. Existing backup archives remain encrypted, isolated and preserved, with no indication of compromise," the company said. ConnectWise called on customers to review their individual Microsoft 365 environments using the company's technical investigation and remediation guide and related information.

Microsoft meanwhile highlighted its own mitigation and protection guidance, which included recommendations like reviewing every Microsoft 365 tenant that might have been tied to ConnectWise and to preserve logs and other forensic evidence before making any changes.

Related:Microsoft's AI Risk Report Misses This Key Detail

Ross Filipek, CISO at Corsica Technologies, says that before reconnecting with ConnectWise, affected organizations should have a clear understanding of what might have happened inside their environment. He pointed to Microsoft's discovery of application credential changes that could give attackers a way back in to compromised environments. Organizations are going to need to investigate whether their Microsoft 365 environments are safe before they reconnect, he says.

"Keep affected connections disabled in line with vendor guidance. Investigate unauthorized changes that could leave another way in. Preserve evidence without delaying containment," Filipek tells Dark Reading. "There's also an immediate business question: Are backups still running? Assign someone on each side to check coverage during the interruption. A restored connection needs verification that backup jobs are completing and recovery works."

Going forward, organizations need to have a recovery plan that takes into account the potential of their losing access to a service that they normally would depend on for recovery, Filipek adds. Incident responders should know which applications connect to the organization's Microsoft 365 tenant and how to quickly sever those connections when necessary, and exercise that scenario with their service provider.

"Establish who checks backup coverage during containment and who decides whether the business can tolerate the interruption. Leaving those responsibilities implied is how both sides end up assuming the other has checked," he says.

Jon Baker, vice president of threat-informed defense at AttackIQ, wants affected organizations to preserve sign-in and audit records and to investigate application sign-ins, Microsoft Graph activity, new credentials, privilege changes, and unusual data access. "Remove confirmed unauthorized access and verify vendor and tenant remediation separately," he advises. "After containment, controlled validation can test whether comparable application behavior can still reach sensitive resources or establish another foothold."

Illinois-based Jai Vijayan is a veteran, award-winning technology journalist with more than 25 years of experience covering cybersecurity. His information security reporting has explored everything from ransomware, nation-state threats, and identity security to AI risk, critical infrastructure protection, software supply chain security, cloud security and emerging enterprise technologies.

Over the course of his career, Jai has written news stories, feature articles, survey reports, white papers, and e-books for enterprise and technology audiences. He has also moderated panel discussions and executive roundtables featuring CISOs, security researchers, and industry leaders.

His work has earned multiple industry honors, including a Joint ASBPE Excellence Award for Best Coverage of Government IT, and a Joint Jesse H. Neal Award for wireless LAN security coverage. Jai holds a Master’s degree in statistics from Bangalore University, and studied broadcasting and electronic communication at Marquette University in Milwaukee.

#10647. NASA just used satellites and debris to navigate without GPS

NASA's Starling mission has reached another milestone in autonomous spaceflight by demonstrating a system that can determine a satellite's orbital position using other objects in space as reference points rather than depending on an external navigation network.

The technology, called FALCON (Fast Autonomous Lost-in-space Catalog-based Optical Navigation), is designed to help spacecraft operate with greater independence. Such capabilities could become increasingly important as NASA pursues missions farther from Earth, including lunar satellite swarms, distributed science missions, and future human exploration.

Satellites near Earth commonly rely on GPS for navigation, but those signals may be weak, unreliable, or unavailable around the Moon and in deep space. FALCON offers an alternative by allowing spacecraft to determine where they are using what they can observe around them.

The FALCON payload is a joint flight experiment developed by NASA and EraDrive, a startup that emerged from Stanford University. The system combines EraDrive's Era-Core flight software and embedded algorithms with Starling's cameras and an onboard catalog of known satellites. Together, these tools enable GPS-independent navigation while also helping the spacecraft track activity and objects in its surroundings.

"FALCON is yet another success for the Starling demonstration mission. The results from FALCON can have far-reaching implications for on-orbit space-traffic monitoring, collision avoidance, and alternative navigation," said Roger Hunter, program manager for NASA's Small Spacecraft and Distributed Systems program at NASA's Ames Research Center in California's Silicon Valley. "The number of 'firsts' from Starling just keeps growing."

Using Satellites and Debris as Reference Points

The FALCON demonstration evaluated two related capabilities using Starling's onboard star tracker cameras. These cameras are standard spacecraft instruments that detect bright objects in space and help determine a spacecraft's orientation and position.

During position, navigation, and timing experiments, FALCON identified objects seen by Starling's cameras, including other spacecraft and orbital debris, and compared them with a publicly available catalog of known space objects maintained by the U.S. Department of War. Once the observed objects were identified and verified, FALCON used them as reference points to calculate Starling's orbit.

A separate set of experiments tested whether the spacecraft could improve orbital estimates for the objects it observed. Mission controllers loaded a catalog containing approximately 20,000 space objects and their predicted orbits onto Starling.

FALCON then compared the catalog information with observations gathered by Starling's cameras. Using those measurements, it calculated Starling's position while also refining the estimated locations of other objects in space. The resulting estimates were even more precise than the existing catalog data.

Over a period of three days, FALCON improved the known orbits of more than 200 objects without any intervention from operators on the ground.

A First for Autonomous Optical Navigation

FALCON's ability to determine its own orbit represents a first for a spacecraft navigating with optical cameras based on its position relative to other objects in space. In separate catalog updating tests, Starling also generated better onboard predictions of object positions than those supplied by ground stations.

These abilities could be especially valuable for future networks of satellites operating without GPS. Coordinated satellite systems may play an important role in supporting human activities on the surfaces of the Moon or Mars.

Precise spacecraft positioning is also essential for distributed science missions, where measurements collected from several locations in space must be accurately aligned. For space traffic management, autonomous navigation and onboard catalog updates could reduce dependence on ground-based tracking networks while improving collision avoidance.

From University Research to Commercial Technology

The FALCON experiment also demonstrates NASA's role in helping university research develop into commercial technology. The work began as a University SmallSat Technology Partnerships project before developing into EraDrive, which is now commercializing its Era-Core software and related hardware for wider use.

Starling gave the technology an opportunity to be tested under real conditions in orbit, demonstrating how advanced flight software can allow satellites to function as increasingly autonomous navigators.

Later this year, Starling, which launched in 2023, will expand the FALCON experiment using Era-Core. The mission's four spacecraft will share tracking information with one another and use those combined observations to refine their positions collectively.

NASA's Ames Research Center in California's Silicon Valley leads the Starling mission. NASA's Small Spacecraft and Distributed Systems program, based at Ames and within the Research and Technology Mission Directorate, funds and manages the Starling mission.

Materials provided by NASA. Note: Content may be edited for style and length.

#10646. State Bank of India Suffers a Customer PII Data Leak

Breaking cybersecurity news, news analysis, commentary, and other content from around the world, with an initial focus on the Middle East & Africa, the Asia Pacific, Europe, and Latin America.

Relatively small data breaches in India can turn quite serious, thanks to a sophisticated underground market for trading PII.

An anonymous hacker has leaked a small batch of sensitive customer records from the State Bank of India (SBI), with potentially serious consequences for the thousands impacted.

SBI has been posting a lot about cybersecurity on social media lately. In August it introduced a new CGI mascot named "Captain Y." Captain Y from SBI is "your Cyber Protector," he says in his promo video, "with awareness as his superpower." SBI's best plug for cybersecurity awareness came on Wednesday, though, when it publicly disclosed that it had suffered a breach of customer data.

In a notice to India's National Stock Exchange, the organization's compliance and company secretary acknowledged that 3,897 customer records had been leaked online. They did not specify whether those records belonged to 3,897 individual customers. In a public notice to customers, the state-run bank emphasized that the incident really only impacted "a very, very small number of customers."

Related:Philippine Migrant Worker Data Likely Leaked in 69GB Government Breach

For a bank that serves north of 500 million people, a few thousand records does indeed qualify as very, very small. Cyber experts note, though, that for those affected, the consequences could be significant thanks to India's sophisticated underground economy for buying and selling personally identifying information (PII).

Last week, a new account with the name "Siriusim" published a post to the mainstream data breach website BreachForums. They had new user data from SBI, they claimed, including personal user information, new account and loan applications, and more. The data included a table with 375,000 rows, and 2,722 PDF files. Importantly, neither figure necessarily indicated the total number of individuals impacted.

As part of the post, Siriusim featured a few documents with handwritten personal information. Mumbai's Free Press Journal verified that PII from the breach samples was valid, belonging to real Indian citizens. One individual, for example, lost their mobile number and know your customer (KYC) documentation in the breach, and the WhatsApp photograph associated with their number matched the passport photo included in the KYC file.

SBI acknowledged that leaked data included names, genders, mobile numbers, email addresses, home addresses, dates of birth, bank profile IDs, metadata associated with loans, and "other files." Follow-on reporting out of Mumbai suggested that this extra data included Central KYC numbers — a single identifier for financial accounts in India — and video KYC verification data, and the kinds of files one might have to submit in the process of creating a new bank account, or filing for a loan. For instance, one published document included an individual's employment and income declaration, with details about their current employer, work experience, and salary.

Related:Russian Influence Operation Widely Targets Latin America

Exactly what precipitated the leak, and why it affected only 0.0008% of the bank's customers, remains unclear. In its formal declaration, SBI emphasized that "the bank's core business functions continue to operate normally without disruptions." Altogether, these clues might point to a breach of some peripheral digital service or data-handling system, rather than the core bank system.

In fact, SBI's last major customer data leak followed just such a script. In 2019, it exposed customer account data through a single server at a Mumbai data center, which was missing password protection. The server supported its "SBI Quick" system, used to text and call customers about basic account information. That one machine put millions of customers at risk, perhaps highlighting just how minor this new leak really is.

"If the data is genuine, the main risk is not direct account theft but credible-sounding phishing, vishing, and identity or loan fraud, since attackers who know someone’s details can impersonate the bank convincingly," explains independent security researcher Sushant Bhardwaj.

Related:Venezuelan Cartel's Malware Honcho Nabbed for ATM Jackpotting

Email addresses, phone numbers, and dates of birth carry fairly obvious risk in the hands of bad actors, and less common kinds of PII can add color to otherwise generic identity attacks. For instance, "KYC details are hard to change, so they can support identity fraud, such as applying for credit in someone else’s name or answering account-verification questions," Bhardwaj notes. And with regard to loan metadata, "a caller who can quote real loan details can pose as the bank or a recovery agent and pressure a borrower into paying a 'fee' or sharing a one-time password (OTP)."

Brian Hussey, senior vice president for Cyderes' Howler Cell, goes deeper. Last month, his team reported on an Indian data broker selling personal records for only about 5 rupees (6 cents or so) per lookup, through a Telegram bot and business application programming interface (API) platform. Using these simple lookups, cybercriminals targeting Indian citizens can obtain vast stores of PII belonging to regular citizens in an instant. And data breaches like SBI's, Hussey notes, can feed into this underground economy. "A breach dump goes stale the day it's posted. A live lookup service is always current, because it is asking the authoritative source in real time. India’s underground data market has both, and they work together," he explains.

"India built one of the most connected identity systems in the world, and an entire industry exists to query it," he warns. "That connectivity is what makes a leak in one place so impactful and useful somewhere else."

Nate Nelson is a journalist and award-winning scriptwriter. In addition to Dark Reading he writes for Darknet Diaries, the most popular show in cybersecurity across all media.

He began his career as a freelancer, ghostwriting Forbes and CNBC op-eds for executives in tech and finance. Then he transitioned to journalism at Threatpost, where he covered cybersecurity news and trends. Throughout those years he co-created a cybersecurity podcast, Malicious Life, which in its day climbed into the Top 20 technology podcasts charts on Apple Podcasts and Spotify.

He holds degrees from New York University and Bard College. As a born and bred New Yorker, he enjoys a superiority complex, but is polite enough to keep it to himself.

#10644. CORS Error Fix: Diagnose Console Errors and Configure Headers

Have 30-200 Employees? Make $50k-$500k selling your data for AI Training.

Have 30-200 Employees? Make $50k-$500k selling your data for AI Training.

Stay up to date with AI tools, model releases, and developer workflows that matter.

Every frontend developer will eventually stare at a CORS error in the browser console, watching an API call fail for reasons that seem opaque. A CORS error fix requires understanding what the browser is actually telling you, matching that specific message to its root cause, and applying a targeted, security-conscious server configuration.

The scheme, host, and port together define an "origin." https://example.com and http://example.com are different origins (different schemes), as are https://example.com and https://api.example.com (different hosts). https://example.com and https://example.com:443 are the same origin because port 443 is the default for HTTPS, and browsers omit it in origin comparisons. The browser enforces the same-origin policy on client-side JavaScript reading responses, not on sending requests. This distinction trips up many developers: the server may still receive and fully process the request; the browser simply refuses to expose the response to the calling code. The request lands, the database row gets written, and the browser throws an error anyway. The policy exists to prevent a malicious page from silently reading sensitive data from another origin using the user's ambient credentials.

Cross-Origin Resource Sharing (CORS) is a controlled opt-in mechanism via HTTP response headers. The server signals to the browser that a specific foreign origin is permitted to read its responses. Four headers control the mechanism: Access-Control-Allow-Origin specifies which origin is allowed, and Access-Control-Allow-Methods declares which HTTP methods are permitted. Access-Control-Allow-Headers lists which custom or non-simple headers the client may send, while Access-Control-Allow-Credentials indicates whether the browser should expose the response to credentialed requests.

The browser does not treat all cross-origin requests equally. "Simple" requests use GET, HEAD, or POST with a Content-Type of application/x-www-form-urlencoded, multipart/form-data, or text/plain, and no custom headers. A POST with Content-Type: application/json is not a simple request and triggers a preflight.

Simple requests go directly to the server, and the browser evaluates the CORS headers on the response. Anything else triggers a preflight request: an OPTIONS call the browser sends automatically before the actual request, asking the server whether the real request would be acceptable. If the OPTIONS response lacks the proper CORS headers, the browser never sends the real request at all.

A typical Chrome DevTools error reads: Access to fetch at 'https://api.example.com/data' from origin 'https://app.example.com' has been blocked by CORS policy: No 'Access-Control-Allow-Origin' header is present on the requested resource.

Two origins appear in this message. The URL after "fetch at" is the target server, the resource the code tried to reach. The value after "from origin" is the page's own origin, the one making the request. Chrome is stating that the target server's response did not include an Access-Control-Allow-Origin header that matches the requesting origin, so the browser blocked the response from reaching JavaScript.

The most common variant is the missing header: No 'Access-Control-Allow-Origin' header is present on the requested resource. The server simply did not include the header at all.

When the console says Response to preflight request doesn't pass access control check, the server either did not respond to the OPTIONS request correctly or returned a non-2xx status code for it.

Redirect variant: Redirect is not allowed for a preflight request. Developers commonly misdiagnose this one. It occurs when the URL triggers a redirect before reaching the application handler. Typical culprits include HTTP-to-HTTPS upgrades, trailing-slash normalization (e.g., /api/data redirecting to /api/data/), or a load balancer rewriting URLs. The browser's preflight OPTIONS request follows the redirect, and the Fetch specification (§4.8) forbids following redirects on preflight requests, so the entire flow fails. Fix the URL so no redirect occurs.

Credential variant: The value of the 'Access-Control-Allow-Origin' header must not be the wildcard '*' when the request's credentials mode is 'include'. When fetch is called with credentials: 'include' or XMLHttpRequest sets withCredentials = true, the server must respond with the exact requesting origin, not *. The browser will block JavaScript access to the response if a wildcard is used with credentials.

Entry point: What does the console error say?

Each branch leads to a specific fix section in this article. Bookmark this decision tree and start here every time a CORS error surfaces.

Before modifying any server code, verify what the server actually returns by simulating a preflight request from the command line:

The -i flag prints response headers. -X OPTIONS sets the HTTP method to OPTIONS, mimicking the browser's preflight. The Origin header declares the requesting origin. Access-Control-Request-Method tells the server which method the real request would use. Access-Control-Request-Headers lists the custom headers the real request would include.

If these are absent, the server is not configured for CORS. If the response is a 301 or 302 redirect, the redirect variant is the culprit.

During local development, the least-configuration way to eliminate cross-origin issues is to proxy API requests through the dev server so the browser sees all traffic as same-origin.

With this configuration, a fetch('/api/users') call from the frontend at http://localhost:5173 is forwarded to http://localhost:3001/users. The browser never sees a cross-origin request. Without changeOrigin: true, the Host header sent upstream retains the dev server's hostname, which may cause backend rejections if the target validates the Host header. This is strictly a development-only solution. Production builds served from a static host will not have this proxy, so proper server-side CORS headers remain necessary.

Tested with: cors@2.8.5, express@4.18, Node.js 20 LTS. The cors package API surface has been stable since 2.x; check the changelog if you are on an earlier major version.

The simplest fix to unblock development uses the cors npm package with its defaults:

This applies Access-Control-Allow-Origin: * to every response. It unblocks any requesting origin, but it cannot be used with credentialed requests, and it exposes every endpoint to every origin on the internet. Any page an attacker controls can issue authenticated requests to your API and read the responses if the user is logged in. Move past it quickly.

For production, validate the incoming Origin header against an allowlist and reflect only permitted origins:

The origin function receives the Origin header value and calls callback(null, true) to allow the request. When true is passed, the cors package automatically reflects the incoming Origin header in the Access-Control-Allow-Origin response header and sets Vary: Origin. This satisfies the credential requirement and prevents open CORS misconfiguration. Setting credentials: true in the options causes the middleware to include the Access-Control-Allow-Credentials: true response header. The cors middleware automatically handles OPTIONS preflight responses when applied at the app level.

Tested with: Next.js 14.x App Router, Node.js 20 LTS. The OPTIONS handler behavior and middleware matcher syntax changed between Next.js 13 and 15; exporting an explicit OPTIONS handler is the safest cross-version approach.

The cors npm package does not plug directly into the Next.js App Router (as of Next.js 13+). Instead, set headers manually in a route handler:

The OPTIONS export explicitly handles preflight requests and returns a 204 No Content with the required CORS headers. Without this, Next.js returns a 405 Method Not Allowed for OPTIONS in some versions (the exact behavior changed between 13 and 14), triggering the preflight failure variant. Exporting an explicit OPTIONS handler is the safest cross-version approach. The getCorsHeaders function returns an empty object for disallowed or absent origins, ensuring that server capabilities (supported methods and headers) are not disclosed to untrusted origins.

For projects with many API routes, centralizing CORS logic in middleware avoids repetition:

The matcher restricts this middleware to API routes only. Access-Control-Max-Age instructs browsers to cache preflight results. Chrome caps this value at 7200 seconds (2 hours); Firefox honors up to 86400. The Vary: Origin header is only set when a cross-origin request is detected (the Origin header is present and allowed), avoiding unnecessary CDN cache fragmentation on same-origin or server-to-server requests. CORS headers including Access-Control-Allow-Methods and Access-Control-Allow-Headers are only sent to allowed origins, preventing server capability disclosure to untrusted origins.

Tested with: Nginx 1.24+. The map directive behavior is stable across modern Nginx versions.

When Nginx sits in front of a backend, it is often the right place to manage CORS centrally. Important: Do not use if with add_header inside a location block -- Nginx's if block causes all parent-scope add_header directives to be silently ignored, breaking CORS headers on actual (non-OPTIONS) API responses.

The map directive builds an allowlist: if $http_origin matches a listed value, $cors_origin is set to that value; otherwise it remains empty. The always parameter ensures headers are added even on error responses (4xx, 5xx), which is critical because Nginx's add_header without always silently drops headers on non-2xx responses.

Nginx's if directive creates a new configuration context. Any add_header inside an if block discards all add_header directives from the enclosing scope.

Why the if block contains all headers and return 204: By placing return 204 inside the if block, the OPTIONS request is fully handled there and never reaches the outer add_header directives or proxy_pass. Non-OPTIONS requests skip the if block entirely and the outer scope's add_header directives and proxy_pass handle them. This separation avoids the inheritance pitfall: each request path (OPTIONS vs. non-OPTIONS) has its own complete, self-contained set of headers.

Note on empty $cors_origin: When the allowlist excludes the origin, $cors_origin resolves to an empty string, and Nginx emits Access-Control-Allow-Origin: (a blank header). Browsers will reject CORS for the request, which is the correct security outcome. However, emitting a blank header is technically non-conformant with RFC 6454. The most robust production solution is to handle CORS in the application layer (Express/Next.js) and have Nginx proxy transparently, or to use OpenResty/Lua for conditional header suppression.

After deploying, verify that both curl -X OPTIONS and curl -X GET against the same URL return the expected CORS headers.

A frequent source of the redirect CORS variant is a proxy_pass trailing-slash mismatch. If the location block is location /api but proxy_pass is http://127.0.0.1:3001 (no trailing slash), Nginx may issue a redirect for /api/ normalization before the request reaches the handler. Similarly, a return 301 https://... rule placed before the CORS location block can redirect the OPTIONS preflight. The fix is straightforward: ensure trailing slashes match between location and proxy_pass, and place any redirect rules after or outside the API location block so they do not intercept OPTIONS requests.

Use an explicit origin allowlist. Avoid * when credentials are involved; the browser will block JavaScript access to the response if a wildcard is used with credentials: 'include'.

Restrict Access-Control-Allow-Methods to only the methods the API actually uses. Listing every HTTP method widens the attack surface unnecessarily.

Set Access-Control-Max-Age to cache preflight responses. Chrome caps this value at 7200 seconds (2 hours); Firefox honors up to 86400 (24 hours). Use 7200 as a safe cross-browser default, or 86400 if your users are primarily on Firefox and you want fewer preflight round-trips.

Include Vary: Origin on every response where Access-Control-Allow-Origin is set conditionally. Without it, CDN or proxy caches may serve a CORS response cached for one origin to a different origin, causing intermittent failures.

Never mirror the request Origin header back without validating it against an allowlist. This is an open CORS misconfiguration that effectively disables the same-origin policy for any attacker-controlled origin.

Do not install browser extensions that disable CORS either -- they mask the problem during development and expose you to real cross-origin attacks on every other site you visit.

Avoid adding CORS headers in both the application framework and Nginx simultaneously. Duplicate Access-Control-Allow-Origin headers cause the browser's CORS origin comparison to fail; the browser receives the response but blocks JavaScript from reading it, producing the same CORS error the fix was meant to resolve.

Read the console error, match it against the decision tree, apply the targeted fix, and verify with the curl preflight command. Use the decision tree above as a reference for every future CORS error.

#10642. IBM quantum computer solves classically intractable problem in 15 minutes

Scientists used a new error correction strategy to encode 70 logical qubits and tackle a problem considered classically intractable.

The quantum computation was completed in about 15 minutes, while leading classical computing methods would require an impractical amount of time to perform the same task.

IBM and researchers at the University of Chicago have announced a quantum computing demonstration that meets key criteria for quantum advantage. The experiment performed a calculation beyond the practical reach of leading classical simulation techniques while also providing evidence that the quantum computer produced a reliable result.

In a new paper, "Sampling hard circuits with verifiably high fidelity," the researchers describe how they achieved both goals using a newly designed form of encoded quantum circuit. The work represents one of the largest demonstrations of logical quantum computing reported so far.

The circuits and experimental results have also been made publicly available through the Quantum Advantage Tracker.

Why Quantum Results Are So Difficult to Verify

Researchers have long used a benchmark called random circuit sampling (RCS) to explore whether quantum computers can outperform conventional machines.

In simplified terms, RCS challenges a quantum computer to generate patterns that become so complicated that a classical computer cannot efficiently reproduce them. That makes the benchmark useful for testing the limits of classical simulation.

But it also creates a major problem. Once the quantum calculation becomes too difficult for a classical computer to reproduce, verifying that the quantum machine actually produced the correct result becomes increasingly difficult as well. Eventually, checking the answer can itself become infeasible unless researchers make strong assumptions about how the quantum computer behaves internally.

The IBM and University of Chicago team approached this verification problem by developing a more structured alternative to RCS.

The researchers showed that their method preserves the same computational hardness criteria associated with RCS, meaning the problem remains extremely difficult for classical computers. At the same time, the added structure allows errors to be detected during the quantum computation.

"Verification remains one of the biggest challenges in firmly establishing experimental quantum advantage," said Bill Fefferman, Associate Professor at the University of Chicago. "This experiment develops techniques to better characterize the fidelity of hard quantum states under noise, increasing confidence that the quantum computer is solving a computationally hard problem."

Soumik Ghosh, PhD student in Fefferman's group at the University of Chicago, added, "Beyond strengthening experimental validation, advances in verification have the potential to unlock practical applications for the next generation of quantum computers."

The experiment also included one of the world's largest-known demonstrations of quantum error correction.

The researchers operated 70 logical qubits. Unlike individual physical qubits, logical qubits are encoded in a way that helps protect quantum information from errors and noise.

Using those logical qubits, the team carried out 2,415 logical two-qubit operations and 468 logical "T gates," two measures that reflect the complexity of the quantum circuit.

The encoded design significantly improved reliability. Effective logical error rates were 10 times lower than the underlying physical error rates, allowing the circuit to maintain unusually high fidelity even while performing a large number of quantum operations.

IBM Says Quantum Advantage Has Entered a New Stage

"We are now firmly in the quantum advantage era," said Jay Gambetta, Director of IBM Research and IBM Fellow. "We have demonstrated a quantum computation beyond the practical reach of classical computers that establishes, with statistical confidence, a lower bound on how faithfully it was executed. This milestone gives scientists, developers, and businesses a new foundation for trusting quantum computers as they scale to problems far beyond what we can achieve classically."

The researchers found that many leading classical simulation methods would face prohibitive runtimes when attempting the same task.

The IBM quantum computer, by comparison, completed the computation in approximately 15 minutes.

A Step Toward Larger, More Trustworthy Quantum Computers

Speed alone is not enough for quantum computing to become useful at larger scales. Researchers also need ways to suppress errors and establish confidence that a quantum system produced a valid result.

This experiment advances both goals at once by combining large-scale logical quantum computing with a method for evaluating the reliability of a calculation that is already beyond practical classical simulation.

Error correction and trustworthy verification are considered essential for scaling quantum computers toward more difficult problems, making the new demonstration an important step toward that goal.

Materials provided by IBM. Note: Content may be edited for style and length.

#10641. The 13 scariest, spookiest video games you should play this Halloween

The nights are drawing in, which can only mean one thing: more bed. But also the impending frights and sights of All Hallow's Eve. Yes, the season of good fear is upon us again, summoning visions of cardboard box robot costumes and other, more devilish things.

And in the spirit of it all, we've crowded around the ouija board to spirit up a list of our horror game favourites - playable on PC, PlayStation 5, Xbox Series X/S, Switch 1 & 2, and VR - that might just sate your macabre appetites this Halloween. Some are scary, some are grim, others offer milder - but no less spooky - chills. We'll be doing a smattering of other spooky stuff as the week goes on, but if you're looking for more recommendations, we did a different horror list last year. And if you've your own favourites, please do share them below!

Platforms: PC, PlayStation 5, Xbox Series X/S, Switch 2

Where better to start then with Resident Evil, one of the granddaddies of survival horror gaming? And Resident Evil Requiem is, as much as anything, a celebration of the series as it turns 30. If Resident Evil is a series of two halves - one part campy action, one part genuine scares - Requiem is the perfect tribute, and when it leans heavily into horror in its sublime opening hours, it's genuinely terrifying. New protagonist Grace Ashcroft is the perfect accompaniment as she leads these first-person segments, roaming a wonderfully atmospheric Rhodes Hill Chronic Care Centre and dealing with some very human zombies who, disturbingly, don't yet seem to realise they're dead. Then comes series stalwart Leon S. Kennedy, roundhouse kicking and quipping to ease the tension in intermittent third-person interludes before it's back into the scares. Eventually, the horror gives way to heavier action, but then go on the party hats for a final stretch of glorious fan-service that feels entirely deserved. It's not only a great Resi game, it's one of the best games this year.

Silent Hill, another grandaddy of the survival horror genre, has always been the moodier of the two big series, trading Resident Evil's B-movie thrills for quieter, more ambient psychological scares. And it's the same story with this year's Silent Hill Townfall, which - continuing the trend established by last year's marvellous Japan-set Silent Hill F - shifts the fog-shrouded action again, this time to a small Scottish island blighted by tragedy. Developer Screen Burn, known for the acclaimed likes of Stories Untold and Observation, takes some big swings here, trading the series' classic third-person perspective for a more intimate first-person one, and shifting the focus from erratic gunplay to stealth. It also tells an unexpectedly gritty and very British tale as it jumps between multiple protagonists. The result is an effective, affecting, and relentlessly suffocating piece of horror. It's not perfect, proving perhaps a bit too relentless, but few series remain this exciting, and so willing to reinvent themselves, after nearly three decades.

Platforms: PC, PlayStation 5, Xbox Series X/S, Switch 2

What Little Nightmares originator Tarsier Studios did next. Having stepped away from the horror series that made its name a few years back, Tarsier returned earlier this year with a fresh macabre offering that, on paper at least, doesn't sound like much of a departure at all. Much like Little Nightmares, Reanimal follows the adventure of two lovable, spindly-limbed moppets - here, Boy and Girl - lost in a hellish, hostile world players traverse by scrambling over platforms, solving light puzzles, and fleeing horrifying entities during the big crescendo moments. What sets it apart, however, is the sumptuous cinematic flair of presentation and a much darker mood: in Reanimal, Little Nightmares' Burton-esque whimsy gives way to a bleaker, more vicious - and undoubtedly more violent - vision that's often genuinely disturbing. That darkness is somewhat alleviated by the comfort of two-player co-op, but however you choose to play, Tarsier's latest is a treat. A game of phenomenal mood and artistry, as striking as it is enigmatic, and a wonderfully grim accompaniment for Halloween.

If the name sounds familiar but the game does not, that might be because developer David Szymanski's Iron Lung was turned into a movie earlier this year by none other than YouTuber Markiplier. And even if you've seen the film adaptation, the original game is worth checking out; it's a masterclass in lo-fi horror that's quite unlike anything else. Early on, Iron Lung seals you into a squalid submersible and plunges you into a blood ocean on a distant alien world. Your goal is to chart its labyrinthine depths - an unknowable expanse of suffocating darkness and silence - searching for several points of interest. The problem? No windows. Instead, you're forced to rely on the tiny, murky image of the world outside beamed onto the submersible's TV screen; the darkness so overbearing, all you can see are the glimpses of strangeness caught in your floodlights. As such, movement becomes a game of blind micro-bursts and cautious rotations, as you sporadically consult your map. That's stressful enough, but Iron Lung plays some clever tricks; its stellar sound design increasingly suggesting something terrible lurks in the darkness. Slowly, the tension reaches suffocating, unbearable heights, and you'll frankly be glad it only takes 45-minutes or so to complete.

Ghost Town's biggest roadblock is the fact it's a VR-exclusive game. But if you've got the means to check it out, it's a gem. Ghost Town is the work of Fireproof Games, and it shares some similarities with the studio's earlier, acclaimed The Room series - particularly in its love of tactile puzzle boxes and contraptions. But Ghost Town is far more ambitious, building a propulsive urban fantasy adventure around its core puzzling, and plunging players into a brilliantly evocative recreation of 1983 London as protagonist and ghost hunter Edith Penrose hunts for her missing brother. As the grimy streets of the capital make way for the craggy seclusion of the North Sea, and, eventually, strange realms beyond, it's wonderfully spooky stuff - full of great writing, captivating world-building, endearing characters, fantastic puzzles, and some magnificently imaginative set-pieces - there's a bit with a lighthouse trapped in time thanks to a troubled spirit that's a real highlight. This one's for you if you've ever suspected dark arts were occurring on the London Underground.

Platforms: PC, PlayStation 5, Xbox Series X/S, Switch 2

It's 1879 and you, private investigator Declan Ward, have been summoned to a remote, rain-lashed corner of western Ireland in search of a young woman named Evelyn Deane. It's a journey that brings you to the titular Blake Manor, now a grand hotel, where the turnips - historically accurate jack-o'-lanterns, if you were wondering - are out in force. We are, you see, three days from All Hallow's Eve, and the hotel is bustling with guests: spiritualists, mentalists, naysayers, and more; here to witness the Grand Séance and a never-before-seen attempt to commune with the dead. All, perhaps, also know something about Evelyn Dean's whereabouts. Soon enough, the detective work begins, and you 'll start sniffing around empty rooms and tantalising corners, searching for discarded notes, newspaper clippings, and other useful clues. You'll also want to interrogate the guests as they move around the house according to their hourly schedule. But every action nudges the clock on further, meaning you'll need to spend your time wisely as awful calamity approaches. Soon new secrets, new mysteries, begin to emerge, and as the clockwork rhythms of day make way for the nightmarish hallucinations of night, is anyone safe?

A tribute to a Doom modder's childhood friend, replicating the family home they used to play together in. As Myhouse.wad creator Veddge explained when he first shared the acclaimed level on the DoomWorld forums back in 2023, an unfinished, work-in-progress version of the house was found on a floppy disc gifted to him inside a box of his dead friend's belongings. A journal included in the download file explains more about the mod's somewhat difficult creation - an endeavour Veddge chose to undertake to honour his friend's memory. But the effort was undoubtedly worth it - as is the slight faff of getting Myhouse.wad to run if you're new to Doom things - and it serves as a simple but touching tribute to friendship across its ten minutes of nostalgic 90s FPS playtime. Only... what's that looking through the window on the ground floor? And was that door in the hallway always there?

Really, you could pluck any Rusty Lake game out of the 18 or so released across the series' ten years of existence, and you'd be in for a grimly macabre treat. But Servant of the Lake is developer Rusty Lake's latest offering, taking players back to 1839, where they've been hired to serve the troubled Vanderboom family across an increasingly strange three-day reunion. Servant of the Lake isn't quite as ambitious as some of the series' other games, such as 2022's excellent co-op mysteryThe Past Within. But what it lacks in structural and narrative experimentation, it makes up for in puzzles, serving up an enjoyably refined take on the series' deceptively clever mix of casual point-and-click adventuring, room-escape-style puzzling, and fascinatingly fragmented, centuries-spanning narrative. And oh yes, it's weird, as its bucolic vistas and gentle bird song gradually give way to blood and butchery, and the comforting logic of reality dims. Sure, it's more darkly amusing than outright disturbing, but Rusty Lake still calls for fresh meat this Halloween.

Probably not one for the faint of heart, Horses gained infamy after being banned by Steam and then Epic Games last year. It all unfolds across two weeks on a farm where humans are kept, masked and naked, in filthy captivity - a grim sight that goes completely unacknowledged for a surprisingly long time as you perform your daily tasks of gardening, woodchopping, and so on to satisfy the farmer's demands. Soon enough, though, Horses charges full-tilt into the grotesque. But while it'll probably make you gasp, and definitely make you squirm; its shocks are comparatively tame. Instead, writer and director Andrea Lucco Borlera's gleefully odd first-person narrative horror - developed in conjunction with Saturnalia studio Santa Ragione - gains its power from its wholly unique ambience, where surreal, slapstick comedy collides with arthouse experimentalism to create a thoroughly destabilising mood. All this, and it has something meaningful to say - not bad for £4.

Platforms: PC, PlayStation 5, Xbox Series X/S, Switch 2

As a game, Hellraiser Revival is wobbly at best, particularly in its opening hours where its wonky gunplay and undercooked stealth never quite coalesce. That means its real-world bits - which include a lengthy stay in a dildo-strewn BDSM club - have a tendency to drag. But when the Labyrinth intermittently calls, developer Sabre Interactive pulls out all the stops. As Hellraiser Revival protagonist Aiden enters this confounding realm - an Escher-esque, non-Euclidean nightmare of piercing chains and endless, impossibly configured stone that serves as home to the Cenobites and their demonic deity Leviathan - the dull, uneven combat gives way to puzzles, platforming, and wonderfully orchestrated pursuit sequences. And it makes the whole thing worthwhile. Slowly, as the line between the Labyrinth and the real-world blurs - and as Saber starts to have more fun with its combat tools - it gets considerably more engaging. Revival and its endless tableaus of horrifically rended flesh are definitely, absolutely not for the squeamish, but Hellraiser fans - and anyone looking for a bit of body horror nastiness - should get a kick out of this one.

Platforms: Meta Quest, PC, PS5, PSVR2, Xbox Series X/S, Switch

Back in 2023, Vertigo Games released a genuinely brilliant remake of developer Trilobytes' seminal 90s CD-ROM adventure, The 7th Guest, for VR. I loved it, and spent many happy hours roaming evil toymaker Henry Stauf's wonderfully eerie mansion, reimagined in new-fangled, fully explorable 3D. Its puzzle made some clever use of VR's 1:1 movement capabilities, and its cast - bringing to life the ill-fated guests of Stauf's macabre soiree - were a blast, hitting exactly the right level of camp and presented using some kind of volumetric witchcraft, letting you walk around their apparitions despite being live-action and FMV. It's great, spooky fun for puzzle fans - even if you're not familiar with the original - but its VR requirements meant it couldn't be enjoyed by all. Well, earlier this year, Vertigo released a non-VR version for Xbox, PS5, and PC. And while it loses a little in translation to flatscreens and standard controls, it's still an enjoyable way to enjoy a cult-classic.

Well, it's solitaire, isn't it? Only, that's not entirely true. Forbidden Solitaire is a clever bit of found media horror, inviting players to explore the titular CD-ROM game - an imagined relic of the short-lived 90s multimedia boom in which the games industry convinced itself the future was lurid colour palettes, awkward pre-rendered polygons, and juddery grainy FMV. Developer Night Signal Entertainment and Grey Alien Games capture the era perfectly as you begin to investigate the enigmatic game, which - as your sister quickly informs you over DM during the game's 2019-set narrative framing device - was embroiled in controversy on release, not least because of its disturbing links to gruesome unexplained deaths. Forbidden Solitaire's fictional history is told across police records, press clippings, 90s local news reports, grisly photos, and even a pitch-perfect VHS recording of a cheesy true-crime-style mystery show. But the majority of your time is spent playing Forbidden Solitaire itself, lost in a ghoulish labyrinth said to grant immortality to those that can reach the end. But of course all is not as it seems. Forbidden Solitaire is a wonderfully creepy haunted media yarn, and - wholly unexpectedly - plays a damn good game of solitaire too.

For a while, it looked like Routine might not make it. First announced in 2012, it vanished into the kind of development hell that rarely results in anything good. But Routine isn't just good, it's great; a cracking first-person sci-fi horror that's got a particularly old-school vibe. Routine's tale of ancient influences and rogue AI takes place on a retro-futuristic lunar resort where the lo-fi 80s tech lends proceedings a disorientatingly anachronistic flavour. Here, adverts for VHS recorders flash up on chunky CRT screens as you ride the sleek transportation train, and the mall, with its futuristic pre-fab curves, meets an explosion of neon and plastic palms. Routine is refreshingly unforthcoming about what to do and where to go; giving you a loose objective, your C.A.T. device - a wonderfully tactile gadget that's half maintenance gun, half PDA - then just sending you off to explore. Unfortunately, the resort is kaput; full of flickering lights and ominous shadows. Still worse are the Terminator-like security bots, always primed to give chase when they spy you - their relentless footsteps reaching a horrifying crescendo behind you. It's a game of claustrophobic stealth and panicked pursuits - and that's just for starters. You're about to have a very bad shift.
