#10575. Cambridge scientists create a $10 chip that could put a medical lab on your wrist

A new optical sensor costing just $10 could bring laboratory-level precision to wearable health monitors, potentially allowing people to track blood glucose without needles. The technology could also transform food testing, industrial quality control, and environmental monitoring.

Researchers at the University of Cambridge and GlitterinTech (a start-up founded by the same research group) have developed a new type of optical spectrometer that combines exceptional accuracy with a remarkably small size and low cost. Measuring just centimeters across, the device could be incorporated into portable electronics and wearable health technology. Its potential applications range from monitoring important health markers in real time to identifying materials and detecting changes in chemical composition.

Optical spectrometers work by analyzing light to reveal information about the substances it interacts with. They are essential tools in medicine, manufacturing, chemical testing, and environmental research. However, making these instruments smaller has traditionally meant compromising their performance. Compact spectrometers often have limited measurement ranges, reduced resolution, or lower accuracy, making them better suited to identifying substances than performing precise measurements.

The researchers believe their new design could overcome these limitations. Known as a convolutional spectrometer, it uses a mathematical principle called the convolution theorem to analyze light in a fundamentally different way. According to the team, this approach delivers performance that surpasses existing types of spectrometers in several key areas, including designs based on light dispersion, Fourier transforms, and computational reconstruction.

A New Way to Analyze Light With Extraordinary Precision

Traditional spectrometers generally separate incoming light into its component wavelengths or use complex calculations to reconstruct its spectrum. The new device takes another approach by performing a mathematical operation called convolution directly on the incoming light.

To accomplish this, the researchers arranged optical components with repeating spectral responses in a sequence. These components can include unbalanced Mach-Zehnder interferometers or micro-ring resonators. By adjusting them in proportion to one another, the system can shift its response to different wavelengths in a controlled, linear fashion. Fast Fourier transforms are then used to accurately recover the light spectrum.

"The key insight was to go back to the mathematics and ask whether there was a fundamentally cleaner way to retrieve spectra," said Dr. Chunhui Yao, a lead author of the study. "By using the convolution theorem directly in the optical domain, we avoid many of the limitations that have held miniaturized spectrometers back. This gives us high precision, strong noise tolerance, and very low computational overhead, all in a compact and low-cost system."

The researchers built the spectrometer using a silicon nitride photonic platform and integrated it with onboard electronics. It operates across a broad range of near-infrared wavelengths (1200-1700 nm) and can collect and process measurements in less than a second.

Another important advantage is its ability to expand its measurement capabilities without major hardware changes. Because the system uses repeating optical patterns, its spectral bandwidth can theoretically be extended almost without limit. Adding more optical components in sequence can also increase its resolution exponentially.

A $10 Sensor That Could Transform Food Testing and Healthcare

To evaluate the device outside purely theoretical measurements, the researchers tested it on a variety of materials and substances. The results demonstrated its potential for applications that normally depend on larger, more expensive laboratory instruments.

When used to identify plastics, pharmaceuticals, coffee, flour, and tea, the spectrometer achieved a 100% classification success rate in the reported tests. It also measured concentrations in water-based and organic solutions with accuracies of approximately 0.01%, exceeding the performance of commercial benchtop spectrometers in those experiments.

The healthcare demonstrations were particularly promising. Under conditions designed to reflect real physiological environments, the device accurately measured several human biomarkers, including skin moisture, blood alcohol, blood lactate, and blood glucose.

The researchers also demonstrated noninvasive glucose tracking over an extended period in one participant. Although further testing would be needed before the technology could become a practical medical product, the finding suggests a possible route toward monitoring blood sugar without repeatedly piercing the skin.

"These biomedical demonstrations are particularly exciting," said Prof. Qixiang Cheng, who led the project. "What makes this work stand out is not just performance in the lab, but technical readiness. Dr. Chunhui Yao's contribution was crucial in translating a mathematical concept into a fully packaged, robust system that operates reliably across temperature extremes and real-world conditions. That combination is what opens the door to practical deployment."

The sensor also demonstrated impressive resistance to temperature changes. It continued operating reliably between -20°C and 80°C, an unusually wide temperature range for a miniature spectrometer. This durability could be especially valuable for wearable devices, factory equipment, and sensors operating outdoors.

Why a Simpler Design Could Be a Major Breakthrough

The new spectrometer's advantages extend beyond its accuracy, size, and price. Its internal design also reduces the amount of computing power needed to analyze incoming light.

Many existing miniature spectrometers depend on complicated calibration procedures and demanding algorithms to reconstruct spectral information. These methods can become unreliable when measurements contain noise, and they often require substantial processing resources.

The Cambridge team's convolution-based approach avoids much of this complexity. Because the measurements follow a linear mathematical relationship, the system can recover spectra rapidly and consistently while using relatively little computational power.

"This is a beautiful example of how elegant engineering can unlock real impact," said Prof. Richard Penty, who contributed to the photonic system design and integration. "The architecture is simple, scalable, and manufacturable, yet it delivers precision that rivals or exceeds much larger instruments. Dr. Chunhui Yao played a central role in bringing together the photonic design, system integration, and experimental validation that made this possible."

Its relatively simple construction could also make the technology easier to manufacture on a large scale, potentially bringing sophisticated optical measurements to devices where conventional spectrometers would be too bulky or expensive.

Bringing Laboratory-Grade Measurements to Everyday Devices

The researchers envision a future in which accurate optical sensing becomes a routine feature of everyday technology rather than something largely confined to specialized laboratories.

In industrial settings, inexpensive spectrometers could be installed throughout manufacturing facilities to continuously check material composition and product quality. Similar sensors could monitor food freshness, identify substances, and analyze environmental conditions on a much larger scale than is currently practical.

Healthcare could see equally significant changes. Compact sensors might eventually enable wearables to measure hydration levels, detect signs of alcohol intoxication, track biomarkers related to physical fitness, or continuously monitor glucose levels for people managing diabetes.

"Our vision is to make spectrometry as ubiquitous as temperature or motion sensing," added Prof. Qixiang Cheng. "This work shows that high-quality spectral information doesn't have to be confined to the laboratory -- it can be embedded directly into the technologies people use every day."

As photonic technology becomes smaller and more advanced, the convolutional spectrometer provides a promising example of how mathematical insights and practical engineering can make sophisticated scientific instruments simpler, cheaper, and more accessible. By combining high precision with a device that costs around $10, the researchers have opened a potential path toward a new generation of smart sensors capable of measuring the hidden chemistry of our bodies and surroundings.

Most teams set up AI visibility tracking for ChatGPT, add Google, and stop there. Claude's audience leans towards the people who research software and services before they buy.

Similarweb put Claude at 3.3% of AI chatbot web visits in February 2026 and 9.2% in May 2026, close to three times the share in three months, while ChatGPT's share kept falling. Prompt volume. 50 to 150 prompts per brand is a realistic start. Fewer than 15 is mostly noise. Check how many prompts the cheaper tiers cover with Claude specifically: on credit-based tools Claude costs more per run, so the entry plan can cover far fewer Claude prompts than the headline number suggests.

Nightwatch is worth a look if you want Claude mentions next to the keyword rankings you already track and you are not paying for one of the large SEO suites. AI tracking is included in the plan price.

#10572. Your company probably saw the problem coming. Here’s why it got blindsided anyway

Most strategic surprises aren’t really surprises. Somebody inside the company almost always saw the signal early. The question is why the organization didn’t do anything useful with those insights while there was still time.

I think of an organization’s early warning capacity as having three parts. Sensing is whether you pick up leading indicators while the signals are still weak. Discipline is whether there’s a consistent process, with dedicated time and people to attend to these signals. Acting is whether you know how to move during what I call the window of optimal warning: late enough that the signal is credible, early enough that you can still shape the outcome.

Depending on how well developed each of these three factors are, you can begin to anticipate where your organization is likely to get into trouble. 

The Cassandra organization: it saw it coming but did nothing

High sensing, weak process, low acting. People see the change and raise the alarm, but nothing happens until it’s too late. 

Kodak is a wildly misunderstood textbook case of this. Kodak didn’t miss digital photography, it invented it. A Kodak engineer, Steve Sasson, built one of the first digital cameras in 1975. In 1981, an internal market intelligence study concluded that digital would eventually displace film, and that Kodak had roughly a decade to prepare. The sensing was excellent. What failed was having the courage to reshape a very profitable core business in the face of the digital inflection point.   

Even worse, under the leadership of Antonio Perez, the company went all-in on printing just as screens were becoming good enough that nobody needed to print any more.  Perez built the printer business at HP but had been passed over for the CEO job.  Many observers thought that billions in investment in printing was mostly a desire for revenge.  As reported by the New York Times in 2011, “Ken Luskin, a disgruntled Kodak investor who runs Intrinsic Value Asset Management, said Mr. Perez’s turnaround strategy was the story of how “a company has been run into the ground by one guy’s ego needs.  He said, ‘I’m going to rub this in Hewlett-Packard’s face.’ This is why they are doing this.”

Kodak filed for bankruptcy in 2012.

Compare this to Fujifilm, which faced the same signals. Under CEO Shigetaka Komori, it squarely faced the reality of the decline of chemical film processing revenue.  It cut deeply and redeployed its chemistry and imaging know-how into medical imaging, pharmaceuticals, cosmetics, and display materials. Same scenarios, completely opposite outcomes.

The fix:  Deploy what I call “tripwires.”  These are leading indicators that, if they all start to point to a similar scenario, your leadership team agrees, ahead of time, on what it will do. To the extent you can, have the debate, the politics and the emotional reckoning before your hand is forced. 

Fast but late: decisive, but only once it’s obvious to everyone

Low sensing, high acting. The organization can mobilize impressively, but only after a change is plain to the whole market.

Microsoft in mobile fits the pattern. When the iPhone launched in 2007, Microsoft’s leadership publicly dismissed it as an expensive niche device. The company’s sensing was tuned to its existing customers (enterprises and PC makers) not to consumers reshaping how technology would fit into their lives.

Once the shift was undeniable, Microsoft acted with real force. It rebuilt its mobile platform from scratch as Windows Phone in 2010 and bought Nokia’s handset business in 2013. But iOS and Android had already locked in developers and users. In 2015, Microsoft wrote off most of the Nokia deal.

Under Satya Nadella, Microsoft got ahead of the shift to cloud and later AI. The same company, with better sensing, played a very different game.

The fix: Mandate that your leaders get out to the edges: non-customers, startups, adjacent industries, and your own front line. Your best customers will be the last source to tell you how the world is changing.

Heroic individuals: the system lives in a few heads

Low discipline, decent sensing and acting. A handful of people carry the early warning function informally. It works brilliantly until they leave, burn out, or get overruled.

Intel under Andy Grove is illustrative. Grove literally wrote the book on strategic inflection points, and Intel’s 1980s exit from memory chips into microprocessors is one of the great pivots in business history. Notably, middle managers had already been shifting factory capacity toward microprocessors before the top team made it official. What saved Intel then was a set of rules that steered capacity allocation at the front lines into the business that would become its future.

But that capability was never fully institutionalized. Paul Otellini, stepping down as CEO in 2013, acknowledged that Intel had passed on making the chip for the original iPhone because the price Apple wanted was below Intel’s forecasted cost. Intel is still reeling from the repercussions. 

The fix: Name owners, protect their time, and put signal reviews on a fixed calendar. If your early warning system disappears if two people depart, you don’t have a system.

Flying blind: ignoring signals until they are unavoidable

Low on all three. Strategy runs on outdated assumptions, the organization only learns about change when it shows up in the numbers and often leadership is more interested in their own short-term gains than the long run health of the organization.

Toys “R” Us was once the category killer that put neighborhood toy stores out of business. Its model rested on assumptions that scale in physical stores was its advantage, and that online was a side channel. 

In 2000, it handed its online sales to Amazon under a 10-year exclusive deal, effectively outsourcing its view of how customers were starting to shop. The partnership collapsed into litigation within a few years. Facing flat sales and falling profits, the Board put the company up for sale in 2004.  A 2005 leveraged buyout then loaded the company with debt, which left little room to experiment just as discounters and e-commerce reshaped toy buying. The company filed for bankruptcy in 2017 and liquidated its U.S. stores in 2018.  The private equity investors did just fine. 

The fix: Well, if your owners don’t care about preparing for the future, as Warren Buffett has argued, probably the best thing you can do is figure out what they do want and build a system around that. Or, as Eric Ries has suggested, turn to a different governance structure for your firm.   

Assuming that your leadership is interested in the longer term, write down the five assumptions your strategy depends on, and pick one leading indicator to monitor for each. It’s a minimum viable early warning system but it’s better than nothing.

What to do if your early warning system isn’t working

If you recognized your own organization in one of these patterns, here’s where I’d start.

Diagnose before you prescribe. Most companies respond to a nasty surprise by buying more data, which only helps if sensing is the problem. Kodak didn’t need more information, it needed more courage and less ego. Find out which of the three capabilities is weakest, and invest there first.

Ask the people furthest from headquarters. In my experience, front-line employees almost always rate their organization’s sensing capabilities lower than senior leaders do and are often astonished at the cluelessness of the folks at headquarters.

Make your assumptions explicit. Every strategy rests on beliefs about customers, technology, regulation, and competitors. If they aren’t written down, nobody notices when they change. Revisit them on a schedule, not just in a crisis.

Decide in advance, then act on less than certainty. The window of optimal warning closes precisely because the evidence keeps getting better. If you wait until you’re sure, you will be sure, and late. Agree now on what you’d do if a key signal crossed a threshold, and set aside a small budget for cheap experiments that test signals before major commitments.

Finally, try one question with your team: What’s the weak signal you’re most worried we’re missing, and what’s the first thing you could do to start watching it? The answers will tell you a lot about what your organization already knows but hasn’t yet said out loud.

#10570. Scientists overcome a hidden obstacle to more powerful quantum computers

Silicon spin qubits could play a major role in the future of quantum computing because they can be produced using the same semiconductor manufacturing methods that make today's computer chips. However, researchers have faced a significant challenge. When multiple silicon qubits are controlled at the same time, their operations tend to become less accurate. Building practical, large quantum computers will require scientists to control many qubits simultaneously while keeping errors to a minimum.

Researchers at the RIKEN Center for Emergent Matter Science and their collaborators have now made important progress toward solving this problem. In a study published in Nature Physics, the team demonstrated highly accurate control of several silicon spin qubits operating simultaneously. Their experiments used an array of five qubits connected to a shared microwave control line. By identifying a major cause of errors during simultaneous operation, the scientists developed a technique to reduce those errors and maintain precision.

Leon Camenzind, a RIKEN research scientist and co-first author who supervised the experiments, explains the significance of the results: "This shows that high-fidelity control can be maintained even when several qubits are operated at the same time and represents an important step toward scaling up silicon-based quantum processors."

Scientists Identify a Hidden Source of Quantum Computing Errors

Unlike conventional computers, which store information as bits representing either 0 or 1, quantum computers use quantum bits, or qubits, that can exist in combinations of both states. Silicon spin qubits store this information using the spin of individual electrons confined within silicon. Performing reliable quantum calculations requires extremely precise control over these electron spins.

Microwave signals provide that control, but operating multiple qubits simultaneously can create unwanted effects that interfere with their accuracy. The researchers traced much of this problem to a phenomenon called the AC Stark shift.

This effect occurs when microwave control signals alter a qubit's effective energy levels, producing changes in the phase of its quantum state. Those phase shifts can disrupt the intended operation of individual qubits, particularly when several are being controlled at once.

To counteract the problem, the team created a calibration method that compensates for these unwanted shifts. Rather than separately calibrating every possible combination of qubits, the technique relies on calibrations performed between pairs of qubits. This makes the approach more practical for systems containing larger numbers of quantum bits.

"Rather than requiring an entirely separate calibration procedure for every possible combination of qubits, our method uses calibrations between pairs of qubits to compensate for the unwanted phase shifts," explains Yi-Hsien Wu, the first author who carried out the experiments as part of his PhD research.

Quantum Qubits Achieve Accuracy Above 99.99%

The researchers combined their calibration technique with an improved device design and carefully adjusted microwave control pulses. Their results showed that exceptionally high accuracy could be maintained even when multiple qubits were operating simultaneously.

When the five qubits were tested individually, each achieved single-qubit gate fidelity well above 99.99%, with the highest approaching 99.999%. Fidelity describes how closely a quantum operation matches its intended result.

The team then tested how well the system performed when several qubits were active together. With as many as three qubits operating simultaneously, fidelity remained above 99.99%. Even when all five qubits were controlled at once, accuracy stayed at approximately 99.9%, approaching the levels needed for practical fault-tolerant quantum computing.

Although the calibration method greatly reduced errors, it did not eliminate them entirely. The researchers found that the remaining loss of accuracy was linked to drive-induced decoherence, an effect caused by the greater microwave power required to operate multiple qubits simultaneously.

Unlike the unwanted phase shifts corrected by the new technique, decoherence involves the loss of the delicate quantum coherence needed for reliable operations.

According to Camenzind, "This is a limitation, but further improvements to device design could help mitigate this source of error."

A New Path Toward Larger Quantum Processors

The findings show that controlling several silicon spin qubits at the same time does not necessarily require a major sacrifice in accuracy. By correcting a key source of errors, the researchers have demonstrated a promising approach for operating more qubits through shared microwave control lines.

This is especially important for the development of large quantum processors. Giving every qubit its own independent control system would make increasingly complex devices difficult to manage. Shared control lines could offer a more practical way to expand these systems while maintaining the precision needed for quantum calculations.

"By addressing a key source of control errors through pairwise calibration," says Camenzind. "Our study supports the use of shared control lines as a practical approach to scaling up quantum processors. Combined with silicon's compatibility with established semiconductor manufacturing, we believe that this advance could help pave the way toward larger quantum processors capable of performing increasingly complex computations."

The broader objective is to develop quantum computers that can reliably perform calculations despite the errors and disturbances that affect quantum systems. Such machines, known as fault-tolerant quantum computers, will require precise, dependable control over large numbers of qubits.

"Our long-term goal is to build a fault-tolerant quantum computer based on silicon spin qubits, and reliable parallel control is an essential step toward that goal," adds Seigo Tarucha, project manager of a silicon quantum computing project under JST's Moonshot Goal 6.

#10569. The biggest tech story of the midterms might be Democrats’ attorney general wins

A blue wave has swept Democrats into control of both the House and Senate, dealing a major blow to Donald Trump in the midterm elections. But beyond the congressional shake-up, a handful of state attorney general races could prove just as consequential for the technology industry.

Democrats won five closely watched attorney general races, including a surprise victory in Texas, where Nathan Johnson defeated Republican Mayes Middleton to become the state’s first Democratic attorney general since 1994. In Arizona, incumbent Kris Mayes defeated Republican Warren Petersen, while Wisconsin’s Josh Kaul secured a third term. Michigan’s Eli Savit defeated Republican Doug Lloyd to succeed term-limited Democrat Dana Nessel, and Democrat Nicole Cannizzaro won Nevada’s open seat.

The results could have huge implications for Big Tech. As federal lawmakers have struggled to rein in the industry, state attorneys general have emerged as some of its most powerful watchdogs, using investigations and lawsuits to force changes to products and practices nationwide. And a change in leadership can bring an abrupt shift in enforcement priorities.

“State attorneys general have become the preeminent regulator and regulatory enforcer in the United States over the last 15 or 20 years,” says Stephen Cobb, partner and vice chair of the state attorneys general practice at Foley & Lardner, a Washington, D.C., law firm. “We’ve seen state attorneys general from across the aisle having an increased focus on the technology industries generally,” he adds.

Why these races matter for Big Tech

Texas, in particular, could signal a major shift. The state’s attorney general’s office has long been among the most influential Republican-led legal operations in the country, regularly helping spearhead multistate lawsuits. Johnson has promised to refocus the office on consumer protection rather than partisan political battles—a change that could reshape the coalitions bringing legal challenges against technology companies.

Arizona and Michigan are also important players in tech enforcement. Arizona has been a key participant in multistate actions targeting the industry, while Michigan has been “actively engaged in national consumer protection and technology matters,” says Brandon J. Smith, partner at law firm Holtzman Vogel.

“A change in attorney general can mean a significant change in enforcement priorities almost overnight, even without a single change in the underlying law,” Smith says.

Attorneys general already have sweeping authority to investigate technology companies, Smith notes. “The technology industry sometimes underestimates just how much authority state attorneys general already possess,” he adds. Even without new AI-specific legislation, state AGs can investigate tech companies using existing consumer protection, unfair and deceptive practices, and antitrust laws.

Tech regulation is increasingly bipartisan

At first glance, the Democratic sweep might seem like bad news for Big Tech. But the partisan dynamics of tech regulation are more complicated, Smith cautions.

Republican attorneys general have generally focused on issues such as alleged censorship and consumer safety, while Democrats have placed greater emphasis on privacy and algorithmic discrimination. But both parties have become increasingly aggressive in their scrutiny of the tech industry, meaning that a Republican victory doesn’t necessarily translate into a friendlier regulatory environment.

“Both parties increasingly view big tech as an industry requiring greater scrutiny,” Smith says. “I don’t think technology companies should interpret partisan disagreement as an indication that either side is going to leave them alone.”

That bipartisan pressure has been particularly evident in efforts to protect children online. Josh Golin, executive director of the children’s advocacy nonprofit Fairplay, points to state AG investigations and lawsuits involving Meta, TikTok, Snap, Discord, and Roblox, which he says have helped push companies to change their products and introduce additional safety features. He expects that scrutiny to continue regardless of which party holds office, given the broad political concern over children’s online safety.

The limits of regulation through litigation

Tech companies are “definitely watching because attorneys general have shown that a single state enforcement can change how that national product works,” says K.J. Bagchi, vice president of U.S. policy and government relations at the Chamber of Progress, a tech industry trade association.

But Bagchi argues that the focus on who occupies these powerful offices obscures a larger problem: State attorneys general have become de facto tech regulators partly because lawmakers have failed to act.

“I would warn against a model where litigation is a substitute for legislation,” he says. “Going after single companies is not necessarily the solution, but it is an understandable byproduct of seeing that the legislative process in some states has fallen apart.”

#10567. AI data centers also lost big in the 2026 midterm elections

President Donald Trump wasn’t on the ballot this midterm election season, but on some tickets, an industry he wholeheartedly supports was: Ballot measures in more than 30 districts across the country asked voters to weigh in on AI data center development.

And data centers lost big. 

Voters overwhelmingly chose to ban or pause local data center development across 38 out of 41 ballot measures. (The other three measures aren’t yet reporting results, according to Ballotpedia.)

The ballot questions varied, in some instances asking voters to prohibit data centers in their cities, and in others, asking them to allow data center development, or even to uphold specific data center deals. 

Where were data centers on the ballot?

Not all results are yet in. But it’s still clear that no matter the framing, data centers lost by landslides.

In Edgewater, Florida, more than 77% of voters approved a ballot initiative to amend the city charter in order to “prohibit the approval, construction, expansion, or operation of new data centers.” 

In Ashville, Ohio, a ballot referendum asked voters to maintain the village’s deal with EdgeConneX for two data centers and on-site natural gas across nearly 200 acres. Residents struck it down with more than 81% of the vote. 

Grove City, Ohio, saw one of the closest races, but it’s still looking bad for data centers. It looks like voters there still chose to rein in data center development—by requiring public approval for certain projects—with 55% of the vote. 

In 28 of the 38 ballot measures for which Ballotpedia is reporting results, support for banning or pausing data center development hit 70% or more. In 13, it hit 80% or more. 

Strong support for data center critics

Data centers didn’t only lose when it came to specific ballot questions, either. Candidates who spoke out against data centers won handily.

In some cases, candidates seemed to sense the public rebuke of data centers early on, and switched their tune.

Democrat Pennsylvania Governor Josh Shapiro, for example, was once in support of the AI data center boom. Then in August he signed an executive order to restrict certain projects and require them to be approved by local officials. 

“We will not be bulldozed by the lawyers working for these big tech companies,” he said at the time, according to NBC News. He won a second term on Tuesday. 

In Georgia, Democrat Keisha Lance Bottoms, who won her race for governor, made a statewide data center pause a key part of her campaign. Georgia is one of the leading states for data center development.

Texas, too, is a major data center hub, with more than 781 data centers either operating, under construction, or planned across nearly 300 campuses, according to Cleanview. 

Outgoing Texas Governor Greg Abbott, who lost his reelection bid, did recently introduce a data center moratorium, but he had backed the industry before, and even raised about $9 million from data center donors. 

Governor-elect Democrat Gina Hinojosa, Abbott’s opponent, called that temporary moratorium a “scam.” She campaigned on data center opposition, promising a new construction moratorium, an end to data center tax breaks, and tighter regulations around water and power use. 

Across both parties, midterm campaigns and outside groups spent more than $173 million in anti-data center ad spending. Democrats led that charge, with $140 million of that spending, versus Republicans with $28 million. 

The data center industry fought back, setting up a super PAC that set aside $1.5 million in ads to supporting Republican Darline Graham, who was fighting to keep her late brother Lindsey Graham’s Senate seat in South Carolina.

She lost to Democrat Annie Andrews in what New York Times reporter Teddy Schleifer called “a black eye for the data-center industry.”

Trump has gone all-in on data centers and AI companies, even writing “let Data Reign” on Truth Social in August. Voters clearly disagree.

#10565. Jeff Bezos praised Raising Cane’s. Its founder built a $22 billion fortune by breaking 3 fast-food rules

Raising Cane’s isn’t following the standard fast-food playbook.

From its limited menu to the employee dress code, founder Todd Graves is charting his own path in a competitive industry. Now, one of the world’s richest men is pointing to his chicken finger empire as a prime example of the power of entrepreneurship.

In a recent Fox News interview, Jeff Bezos pushed back on the notion that building a successful business and becoming a billionaire made someone a villain.

Instead, he pointed to entrepreneurs who expanded their companies and created thousands of jobs. For the Amazon founder, Graves is a prime example of that.

“There’s nothing wrong with making unbelievably good chicken that people love,” he said. “And it doesn’t make him a bad person.”

However, although Graves and Bezos are both billionaires, the former followed a different playbook than the latter.

In 1996, Graves, who was 24, opened the first Raising Cane’s in Baton Rouge, Louisiana. He used loans from friends, family, and the Small Business Administration, as well as savings from his jobs as a boilermaker and an Alaskan salmon fisherman.

Three decades later, the ethos of the fast-food chain remains the same: a simple menu centered on chicken fingers, fries, coleslaw, Texas toast, and Cane’s Sauce.

Even now, the smallest change, such as the addition of a sandwich combo, can create anxiety and stress.

“To tell you the truth, man, I kind of wish we didn’t even have it on the menu. It’s like 3 or 4 percent of sales. And it slows us down,” Graves previously told Inc. “I wish we didn’t have it, but I won’t take it away now.”

This small admission reflects the chicken chain’s broader philosophy. While Bezos launched a publicly traded giant, Graves has focused on keeping Raising Cane’s limited in scope and tightly controlled.

Keeping the company private

The biggest difference between the two billionaires may be their views on taking a company public.

Forbes estimates Graves currently owns about 92 percent of the company, with a net worth of approximately $22 billion. The founder has said Raising Cane’s has no plans to go public, a choice he has tied to preserving the chain’s culture.

A key executive has echoed the same sentiment. “We have no plans on that,” AJ Kumaran, the company’s co-CEO and COO, told Restaurant Business. “We are privately held because we want to remain that way.”

By comparison, Bezos took Amazon public just three years after its founding. It debuted on the stock market in May 1997 at $18 a share, raising $54 million to fuel its growth.

Focusing on employees

However, even though Graves is committed to retaining control of the business, he takes a more relaxed approach with his employees.

At Raising Cane’s, crew members wear casual uniforms and music has been allowed in the kitchen since the early days. It is a deliberately relaxed approach that stands apart from Amazon’s more regimented structure.

A commitment to charity

Yet, even amid their differing approaches to business, both Bezos and Graves are committed to charitable giving.

Bezos’s Earth Fund, backed by a $10 billion pledge, has distributed about $2.4 billion to date. His Day 1 Families Fund has donated more than $850 million to nonprofits addressing homelessness.

After the Texas floods in 2025, Graves donated $1 million to the Red Cross. In August, Graves told Dallas Weekly that the company had given more than $165 million to charitable causes over its first 30 years, something he hopes will continue.

Raising Cane’s didn’t immediately respond to a request from Inc. for comment.

—Amaya Nichole

This article originally appeared on Fast Company’s sister website, Inc.com. 

Inc. is the voice of the American entrepreneur. We inspire, inform, and document the most fascinating people in business: the risk-takers, the innovators, and the ultra-driven go-getters that represent the most dynamic force in the American economy.

#10564. Tiny magnetic vortices could help computers work more like your brain

Tiny magnetic structures called skyrmions could help pave the way for a new generation of computers that process information more like the human brain while using far less electricity. Although most people have never heard of skyrmions, these microscopic magnetic vortices may eventually play an important role in how computers store and process data.

A study published in the journal Nature Nanotechnology provides new insights into how skyrmions behave and how scientists can control them. The findings could help researchers develop smaller, more efficient computing systems and advance emerging quantum technologies.

Most of the research was conducted at the Institute of Physics at Johannes Gutenberg University in Mainz, Germany, with contributions from a professor at the Norwegian University of Science and Technology (NTNU).

"Skyrmions are small, magnetic vortices that can store information in a completely new way," explained Asle Sudbø, who leads NTNU's Centre for Quantum Spintronics (QuSpin).

Unlike conventional technologies, which require increasing amounts of space and energy to handle growing quantities of data, skyrmions could offer a much more efficient alternative.

"Instead of the current technology, where we constantly need more space and energy to process data, skyrmions could make it possible to build much smaller and more energy-efficient data storage systems," explained Sudbø.

Tiny Magnetic Vortices Could Enable Brain-Like Computers

The potential applications of skyrmions extend well beyond conventional data storage. They are also important to spintronics, which explores ways to use the magnetic properties of electrons in electronic devices, and to research involving topological quantum effects.

One particularly promising possibility is the development of computers that operate in ways similar to biological brains.

"These nanoscale vortices could help develop computers that resemble biological brains," said Sudbø.

Rather than relying on conventional transistor-based computing, such systems could use magnetism to process information. In principle, this approach could dramatically reduce electricity consumption, potentially allowing future computers to perform complex tasks with very little energy.

Turning that possibility into practical technology, however, requires scientists to understand exactly how skyrmions behave and how to manipulate them reliably.

The latest research represents an important advance toward that goal.

Scientists Film Magnetic Skyrmion Lattices Melting for the First Time

Skyrmions do not always exist as isolated magnetic structures. Under certain conditions, they organize themselves into repeating patterns known as lattices, resembling the orderly arrangement of atoms in a crystal, but on a much smaller scale.

Scientists can manipulate these arrangements, a capability that could be essential for using skyrmions in future computing devices.

In the new study, researchers achieved something that had not been demonstrated before. They recorded the melting of a magnetic skyrmion lattice as it happened while simultaneously controlling individual skyrmions.

"For the first time, researchers have managed to film how a magnetic skyrmion lattice melts in real time, while simultaneously being able to manipulate each individual skyrmion directly as they film it. For example, both their shape and size can be changed 'on the fly'," said Sudbø.

The ability to observe this process directly provides a clearer picture of how skyrmions respond when their organized structures break apart. It also allows researchers to study how changing the size and shape of individual magnetic vortices affects their behavior.

A New Step Toward Energy-Efficient Computing

Understanding how skyrmions behave during the breakdown of their lattices could help scientists develop more precise ways to control them. That control is particularly important if these magnetic structures are to become useful components in future computer systems.

The findings therefore offer more than a new way to observe an unusual magnetic phenomenon. They provide information that could help researchers overcome challenges involved in developing practical skyrmion-based technologies.

"The findings give us new insight into how these types of particles behave. This could therefore become important for the development of more energy-efficient computer technology in the future," said Sudbø.

Although substantial development is still needed before skyrmions can be used in everyday computing devices, the research highlights their potential for improving data storage, enabling new computing architectures, and supporting advances in quantum technology.

By learning to observe and manipulate these tiny magnetic vortices in real time, scientists are gaining capabilities that could eventually help reshape the design of computers.

"This could revolutionize the way we think about computers," concluded Sudbø.

Materials provided by Norwegian University of Science and Technology. Original written by Steinar Brandslet. Note: Content may be edited for style and length.

#10562. CVS is splitting into two companies: Healthcare giant’s ‘Pharmacy’ breakup explained

CVS is breaking up.

On Wednesday, the healthcare giant announced plans to split into two separate, independent companies, and both will be publicly traded. 

The two companies will form a “leading healthcare solutions company” called CVS Health, and will encompass Aetna, CVS Caremark, CVS Specialty, Oak Street Health, and Signify Health.

The second company, dubbed CVS Pharmacy, will be made up of roughly 9,000 CVS pharmacies, mail pharmacy, MinuteClinic, and the Health100 tech services business.

The company also announced that current CVS Health chair and CEO David Joyner will serve as CEO of the “new” CVS Health, and Prem Shah, current Group President of CVS Health, will be the CEO of the “new” CVS Pharmacy.

“Our history is defined by proactively evolving to stay ahead of what’s next in healthcare, and in today’s environment, that means delivering more affordability, greater access, and a simpler experience,” said Joyner in a statement. “From a position of strength, and a focus on the long term, we plan to create two focused companies to improve consumer engagement, affordability, and care coordination.”

CVS shares were down approximately 12% on Wednesday morning.

As for the reason for the split?

Notably, the move effectively reverses, in some respects, the 2018 merger between CVS Health and Aetna.

According to company leadership, two smaller companies would be able to be more efficient and nimble than one single, larger one. When the dust settles, CVS Pharmacy will basically be a pharmacy company, while CVS Health will be focused on insurance and other services.

Regulatory concerns may also be at play. For example, The New York Times reports that some states, such as Arkansas and Tennessee, have passed laws in recent years that prevent large conglomerates from managing prescription benefits while simultaneously running retail and mail-order pharmacy services. 

Other companies have taken on similar strategies in recent years. Notably, Comcast is breaking off its media and technology businesses, it announced earlier this year, which likewise follows NBCUniversal’s decision to spin off some of its brands into another company, Versant.

Further, Madison Square Garden Sports is spinning off its pro sports franchises (the NHL’s New York Rangers and the NBA’s New York Knicks) into separate companies. And Keurig Dr Pepper recently announced plans to spin off its coffee division.

#10561. 8 Checks Developers Should Add Before Importing PDF Tables into an Application

Have 30-200 Employees? Make $50k-$500k selling your data for AI Training.

Have 30-200 Employees? Make $50k-$500k selling your data for AI Training.

Stay up to date with AI tools, model releases, and developer workflows that matter.

A PDF table can look correct and still produce unreliable application data. A wrapped description becomes two rows. An account code loses its leading zeros. A repeated page header is imported as a transaction. A missing decimal separator changes an amount without triggering an obvious error.

These problems are easy to overlook when an exported spreadsheet opens successfully. But opening a workbook proves very little about whether its contents belong in a database.

For developers building reporting dashboards, inventory systems, or document-import features, PDF extraction should feed a validation workflow. The following eight checks help separate readable output from data your application can safely process.

The examples use fictional invoice-style records and Python. They demonstrate a narrow validation contract rather than a complete PDF conversion service.

Not all PDFs contain the same kind of information.

A digitally generated document may include selectable text and vector lines. A scanned document may contain only page images. A mixed document can contain both, sometimes with an existing OCR layer that is incomplete or inaccurate.

Inspect representative pages before committing to an extraction strategy. Check whether text is selectable, whether copied Check parsing and validation behavior against fixtures

The pdfplumber documentation explains its text and table capabilities, including visual debugging. Its strengths are primarily associated with machine-generated PDFs; it is not an OCR engine.

OCRmyPDF adds a searchable text layer to scans. That does not, by itself, reconstruct a correct table schema. You still need to determine which text belongs in each row and column.

Practical check: Build a sample set containing a clean digital PDF, a scan, and a multi-page table before evaluating the extraction path.

A conversion step should create an inspectable intermediate result. It should not automatically authorize database writes.

For workflows that need a spreadsheet as the intermediate format, Lido is one option for converting PDF content to Excel. Evaluate the output against representative documents, then apply the same schema and reconciliation checks you would use with a custom extraction script.

Commit accepted records to the application.

This structure lets you replace an extraction tool without changing every downstream rule. It also provides a place to inspect failures before they become production records.

SitePoint’s guide to parsing spreadsheet data with Python provides background on working with spreadsheet formats in an application workflow.

Practical check: The importer should be able to reject a workbook even when conversion completed successfully.

Column names alone are not a sufficient contract. A field called “Date” could represent an invoice date, payment date, or service date.

Decide how repeated headers, subtotal rows, footnotes, and blank lines will be identified. Do not let them disappear through undocumented cleanup rules.

Load a workbook with deliberate type handling

The pandas read_excel reference documents these loading options. Using strings limits unwanted interpretation at this stage, while keep_default_na=False preserves values that would otherwise match default missing-value markers.

However, reading a cell as text cannot recover information already lost upstream. If a converter stored 00127 as the number 127, this setting will not reconstruct the original ID.

Practical check: Compare identifiers against the original document, including examples with leading zeros.

Removing every comma and currency symbol may look convenient, but it hides ambiguity. The strings follow different conventions.

Choose an explicit format per document family. The following parser accepts a deliberately narrow format: ASCII digits, optional correctly grouped thousands commas, a decimal point, and up to two decimal places. It permits a leading minus sign for adjustments.

This intentionally rejects parentheses, currency symbols, exponent notation, and comma-decimal formatting. Those formats may be valid in other documents, but supporting them requires an explicit rule.

Python’s Decimal documentation explains decimal arithmetic. Constructing a Decimal directly from the validated string avoids first introducing a binary floating-point representation.

Practical check: Keep the original extracted value alongside the normalized value, and reconcile the result against other evidence.

A hundred extracted rows are not necessarily the correct hundred rows. One line may be missing while another is duplicated.

Required fields are present and nonempty.

Dates are valid under the declared format.

Line identifiers are unique within the correct scope.

Recognized line-item totals reconcile with the appropriate subtotal.

Each accepted row has a traceable source location.

For a document whose stated subtotal is exactly the sum of its line amounts:

Do not compare that subtotal directly with a grand total containing tax, shipping, or other adjustments. First model those components.

Avoid a generic tolerance such as “accept differences below one dollar.” If the document requires rounding, define where rounding occurs, the currency precision, and the permitted discrepancy.

SitePoint’s overview of data preprocessing provides additional context for separating cleaning, transformation, and integration.

Practical check: Inject one missing row and one duplicate into your fixtures. Confirm that the workflow detects both.

When a record fails validation, a reviewer should not have to search a long PDF without context.

Keep a reference to the source document, page number, extraction run, and original field value. Where the extractor exposes cell coordinates, retain them so a review interface can highlight the relevant region.

Distinguish “not extracted,” “blank in source,” and “not applicable.” Turning all three into an empty string makes it harder to understand what happened.

Confidence scores can help prioritize work, but they are not interchangeable across tools and do not replace business validation. A highly confident extraction can still be placed in the wrong column.

Practical check: Ask someone unfamiliar with the document to resolve a flagged record using only the review interface and its source reference.

An import may stop after extraction, during validation, or while writing records. Retrying should not create another copy of every accepted line.

Assign each import a stable identity. A document hash can help identify byte-identical uploads, while an explicit tenant or account scope prevents unrelated users’ imports from being treated as one.

A hash alone is insufficient for every duplicate policy. Two differently encoded PDFs may represent the same invoice, and one file may legitimately need reprocessing after a parser correction.

Track both the document identity and processing version. Separate extraction attempts from committed business records.

At the database boundary, define the appropriate uniqueness rule and use a transaction for the unit you promise to import atomically. For example, invoice lines might be unique by account, invoice identity, and line number—not by invoice ID alone across all customers.

When reprocessing changes existing values, make that an explicit replacement or correction workflow rather than an unnoticed side effect of retrying.

Practical check: Run the same accepted import twice and verify that the application record count remains unchanged.

The most valuable fixtures are not always the most visually complicated. A tiny change can alter business meaning while producing valid-looking data.

Use pytest parameterization to exercise numeric-format boundarie. SitePoint’s Python unit-testing guide explains the broader testing workflow.

Parser tests do not verify the extraction engine. Add end-to-end fixtures with manually verified expected records for repeated headers, wrapped descriptions, scans, and multi-page tables.

Measure field accuracy and the number of documents that pass all required checks. A strong average can conceal a weak result on the one field your application depends on most.

Practical check: Retain a regression fixture for every meaningful production failure, using synthetic or appropriately sanitized documents.

PDF conversion produces candidate data. Your application decides whether that data is complete, consistent, and suitable for use.

A dependable workflow identifies the source format, preserves extraction evidence, enforces explicit column rules, reconciles values, and makes retries predictable.

Start with one document family and a small verified fixture set. Expand only when you can explain both why a record was accepted and how a reviewer can investigate one that was rejected.

#10559. How AI impacts solopreneurs’ relationships with their clients (and what to do about it)

Most people I know have asked themselves some version of “Is AI replacing me?” It’s a fair question. 

But, running a solo business, I think the question extends beyond “Is AI replacing the work I do?” It’s also impacted the way clients interact with the people they hire. 

Clients expect AI to make your work cheaper

Some companies are really moving their budgets away from hiring people to AI. The Ramp Economics Lab tracked how businesses split their spending between freelance marketplaces and AI model providers. Among the companies it studied, the share of spend going to freelance marketplaces dropped from 0.66% in the fourth quarter of 2021 to 0.14% in the third quarter of 2025. Over the same time period, the share going to AI model providers climbed from zero to nearly 3%.

How far that shift goes varies from company to company and the type of service provided. But clients know AI is cheaper (Ramp’s data bears that out). As a result, some clients may expect to pay less for human work. I suspect this is because they think that if AI allows the solopreneur to work faster, then they, the client, should get some benefit. 

I don’t think solopreneurs should drop their rates to compete with AI, because that devalues the end result that the client is paying for. If a client’s budget has shrunk, you might cut the scope before you reduce your rates. You could also offer more flexible terms, like ad hoc or on-demand work, so a client with a tight budget can still bring you in when they need you.

When a client runs your work through AI

Clients now have a free “second opinion” on everything you deliver. They can paste your work into a chatbot and ask for a critique, and the answer will sound confident (even if it’s confidently wrong). AI feedback also tends to be generic. It can misunderstand the project’s goals or what the client hired you for—forcing you to respond to a robot’s assessment.

It helps to cover AI upfront, either during a discovery call or in the contract. You might explain how you use AI yourself and how you respond to requests for changes to the deliverables.

I know some solopreneurs who let clients know that they won’t consider AI-generated feedback, like a long email that was clearly written by AI. Whether or not you go that far, the scope of the project should clearly limit how much feedback gets incorporated into any revisions you make.

Getting found when everyone’s outreach sounds like AI

Cold pitches and social posts are now full of AI-generated content, so the usual ways of finding clients don’t work as well.

I’m on the receiving end of many cold pitches, and my inbox is now flooded with emails written by AI. I also used to find clients for my business through LinkedIn, but it feels impossible at times to stand out among the “noise.”

These days, personal connections reign supreme. It feels like the only surefire way to make sure you break through the AI content: having people who know you, understand what you do, can vouch for your work, and are willing to refer you.

The effort it takes to connect with people on a human level also goes further when so much of the outreach around you sounds like it came from the same template.

The clients worth keeping want a human collaborator

The people and companies trying to replace work with AI aren’t necessarily a fit for you anyway. They don’t value the human aspect of that particular type of work, and you’re not going to convince them otherwise. It might mean the pool of potential clients is smaller, in addition to a more challenging environment to find clients in the first place. Put it all together, and it’s a stressful time to run a business.

But if you can find the right clients, they’ll appreciate you more. My own clients hire me for judgment and expertise, and they still want a person behind that work.

#10558. Outback Steakhouse store closures: See a list of doomed locations as franchisee files for bankruptcy

A number of Outback Steakhouse locations closed their doors last month in the lead-up to a bankruptcy petition by one of the casual dining chain’s largest franchisees, court documents reveal. The store closures span four states. Here’s what to know.

What’s happened?

Cerca Trova Restaurant Group Holdings, which operates as Out West Restaurant Group, one of Outback Steakhouse’s largest franchisees, sought Chapter 11 bankruptcy protection in the United States Bankruptcy Court for the District of Delaware on Monday.

The San Diego-based company, which currently employs around 3,669 workers, operates 61 Outback Steakhouse restaurants across Arizona, California, Colorado, Nevada, and New Mexico.

Outback Steakhouse, the dining chain known for its Australian theme, had more than 660 U.S. restaurants as of the end of last year, according to parent company Bloomin’ Brands.

Why did Cerca Trova file for bankruptcy?

Court records show the franchisee filed for bankruptcy to sell the majority of its assets.

However, that same day, Cerca Trova filed a motion to reject the leases on 10 restaurant locations that it had closed between October 11 and October 25.

According to court documents, the shuttered restaurants operated at a loss or at margins insufficient to cover their occupancy costs. These locations aren’t part of the proposed sale. 

Which Outback Steakhouse locations recently closed?

The following Outback Steakhouse locations closed in October.

Arizona

  • 4871 E. Grant Road, Tucson
  • 1860 E. McKellips Road, Mesa

California

  • 7575 Beach Blvd., Buena Park
  • 25261 N. The Old Road, Valencia
  • 26652 Portola Parkway, Foothill Ranch

Colorado

  • 7065 Commerce Center Drive, Colorado Springs
  • 15 W. Springer Drive, Highlands Ranch
  • 2066 S. Abilene St., Aurora
  • 8601 W. Cross Drive, Littleton

Nevada

  • 3645 S. Virginia St., Reno

The franchisee had previously closed three underperforming locations earlier this year, court documents show.

Growing financial pressure since 2018

In court documents, the company noted that it has faced growing financial challenges since 2018 due to declining traffic and rising labor costs.

In 2020, during the COVID-19 pandemic, its revenue dropped around 35%. Cerca Trova has pursued a sale four times since 2018.

The company cited declining traffic and earnings—along with rising labor, food, and production costs—as the drivers of the mounting financial pressures that led to its recent bankruptcy filing.

On November 1, Bloomin’ Brands entered into a purchase agreement to acquire all of Cerca Trova’s assets for $26.3 million, subject to competing higher offers. The majority of Outback Steakhouse locations are already company-owned.

Fast Company reached out to Bloomin’ Brands to ask whether it plans to reopen any of the recently closed locations. We’ll update the story if we receive a reply.

#10556. AI Tools Are Generating Massive Attacks for Little Cost

One campaign targets 105 sites using open-weight models; in another, public models gained full domain control for $12. Cyber-defense will have to change.

Over five days in September, a Chinese-speaking attacker used three different AI harnesses and both open-weight and public AI models to target 105 different e-commerce sites.

Usually within a day, and often with hours, the autonomous hacking system compromised at least 27 different companies. Malicious agents stole at least 600,000 payment card records from two, installed credit-card skimmers on the websites of five, and gained some degree of illicit access to the rest, which includes at least one Fortune 500 company, according to Gambit Security, which discovered the campaign.

The total bill for the attackers? An average of $25.46 per completed target.

"The scale and success of this campaign are remarkable for just one week, especially considering the size of some of the victims," says Sa'ar Elias, co-founder and chief research officer for Gambit Security. "Work that would previously have required a coordinated team of skilled attackers can now be carried out by one person without much prior knowledge."

Related:Incidents Move Too Fast for Pen & Paper

The autonomous credit-card and data-stealing campaign is not an outlier. Agentic AI has sped up vulnerability research, leading to a massive surge in CVE assignments. Attackers are increasingly using AI to automate attacks, exploit systems faster, and even act as fully autonomous hackers.

In another instance, researchers with AI cyber-defense firm Silverfort conduct lab tests using an orchestrating agent and publicly available versions of Claude Opus to explore how quickly autonomous AI can turn initial access into a full compromise. The "attacker" gained complete domain control in eight minutes, says Colin Ferris, threat hunting and incident response lead at Silverfort.

"The barrier to entry is falling," Ferris says. "What it takes is a basic foothold, not exotic skill, and that’s why this won't stay confined to sophisticated actors."

Prices in dark markets have reflected the reduction in costs for attackers. Because of increasing supply in the underground markets, the average price of sold initial access declined from just over $1,400 to $429, according to figures from threat intelligence firm Flashpoint. While fewer companies are paying ransoms — 28% in the first half of 2026 — ransomware activity continued to grow by 45%, the company said.

"Initial access is where we've measured the price drop," says Ian Gray, vice president of intelligence for Flashpoint. "Elsewhere in the attack chain, we see AI making operations faster and easier to scale."

Related:Germany Busts 'Crime-as-a-Service' Investment Fraud Outfit

In many ways, the situation resembles the one on current battlefields: Cheap autonomous or directed attacks by drones are making expensive defenses uneconomical, which means that defenders have to find cheaper ways to defend and harden systems. In the latest campaign, cyberattackers used the agentic AI system Hermes and two AI penetration-testing frameworks, Strix and Cairn, according to Gambit Security.

"Attackers can now launch increasingly sophisticated attacks at very low marginal costs, while defenders must maintain a high level of reliability across complex environments," says Gambit Security's Elias. "Defending against every individual attempt can quickly become an unsustainable economic proposition."

Applying AI to existing security processes will be necessary, but not enough, he says. Instead, companies need to look at their business processes, determine which ones matter most, and find ways to protect them and prevent disruption.

For the past two decades, cybersecurity experts have warned that companies can't expect to avoid attacks simply because they are in an obscure business or have a relatively small attack surface. Every part of a company that is attached to the Internet or connected to a partner connected to the Internet will be attacked, says Albert Ziegler, chief information security officer at offensive cybersecurity firm XBOW.

Related:Investors Dish on New Startups & What They'd Back Next

"These are not incredibly expensive attacks, but also these are attacks that work because the sites haven't been hardened enough," he says. "It's that it's not enough to protect a couple of crown jewel sites that you are very concerned about."

One way to bolster defenses is to focus on the basic paths that AI agents tend to exploit — overprivileged accounts, reused credentials, and unmanaged service accounts — and automate access decisions, so humans do not slow down responses, Silverfort's Ferris says. When Silverfort researchers improved controls, especially authentication and access, the same agent that took the domain in minutes hit 21 dead ends and gave up, he says.

"AI didn't create these weaknesses; it just finds them faster," Ferris says. "Controls that stop the attack at the point of access are cheaper than cleanup afterwards."

Companies should focus on the economics of recovering from an attack and how to protect their minimum viable business processes, says Gambit Security's Elias. Business leaders should focus on what investments will have the most business impact.

Unfortunately, that may mean budgets need to grow to adapt to the economics of AI, he says. However, "spending should increasingly be measured by how effectively it protects business operations," he notes, "rather than simply how many threats or tools a security program can manage."

Rob is an award-winning, veteran technology journalist of more than 30 years, reporting on global cybersecurity issues, the latest offensive and defensive technologies, malware incidents, cyber conflict, and AI's impact on software and cybersecurity.

A former research engineer, Rob has written for more than two dozen publications, including CNET News.com, Dark Reading, MIT's Technology Review, Popular Science, and Wired News. He has received five awards for journalism, including Best Deadline Journalism (Online) in 2003 for his coverage of the Blaster worm. Rob also analyzes data on various trends using Python and R for both his reporting and his clients. Recent reports include analyses of the shortage in cybersecurity workers, annual vulnerability trends, and annual threat reports.

Rob holds degrees from Cornell University in Electrical Engineering and Computer Science (double major).

#10555. Uber CEO Dara Khosrowshahi: Midterms sent a ‘very clear message’

Uber CEO Dara Khosrowshahi said this morning that Democrats’ sweeping midterm victory sent a “very clear message” about the damage inflation has done to American consumers.  

During an appearance on CNBC’s Squawk Box, Khosrowshahi said the problem stems from how the economy has evolved since the 2008 financial crisis, as wages have not kept pace with skyrocketing prices.

“When you look at capitalism, there’s capital investment and return on capital, and obviously there’s return on labor,” he said. “If you look over the past 20 years, return on capital has increased very, very significantly. You can’t say the same thing about return on labor.”

The rise of artificial intelligence is only adding to workers’ anxiety, he added.

“AI is an instantiation of capital where, to some extent, capital could replace labor as well, which is rightfully, in some cases, scaring people,” Khosrowshahi said. “But it’s also very, very powerful in its potential.”

Khosrowshahi said he was sharing his opinion and that he is “not a politician.”

When asked how politicians and business leaders should respond, Khosrowshahi pointed to the tax code.

“[The fact that] capital gains are taxed at a lower rate than regular income makes no sense to me,” Khosrowshahi said. “They should be balanced.”

“Whether you should raise one or lower the other one, that’s really up to the folks in power,” he added. “But it doesn’t seem right to me.”

Khosrowshahi has led Uber since 2017, when he replaced cofounder Travis Kalanick amid a series of scandals involving the company’s workplace culture and leadership. Khosrowshahi was previously the CEO of online travel company Expedia.

Uber employs millions of drivers and couriers who work as independent contractors.

Khosrowshahi’s comments came on the same day Uber reported $14.8 billion in third-quarter revenue, up 10% from a year earlier, and $1.4 billion in operating income, up 30%.

The company also said it expects to have about 700 fully driverless vehicles operating on its platform by year-end.

#10553. Apple is restricting a fast-growing category of apps. Here’s what users need to know

Apple is about to put greater restrictions on dating apps and AI companions. 

Starting on November 16, the company will require developers to declare whether their apps use AI to facilitate romantic connections. The apps that do use artificial intelligence—whether it’s an AI companion or technology that assists humans in connecting with one another—will only be allowed for users older than 18. 

According to Apple’s November 2 announcement, apps will have to declare whether they offer real-world location sharing, as well as “features that enable dating or relationship connections between real people and/or a virtual companion that engages a user in sexual or romantic content.”

In addition, the announcement stated that app creators “must provide these declarations when submitting an app update or making changes to your age-rating questionnaire.” It noted that the declarations must be complete by January 12, and said that all apps using the technology must have a minimum age rating of 18-plus. 

In some places, location sharing won’t automatically impact minimum age restrictions, such as in Brazil, where regulations only require an above-16 rating. 

Dating apps have been widely adopting AI to assist romance-seekers in making connections. Apps like Hinge, Tinder, and Bumble use AI for tasks like helping with profile creation, choosing photos, suggesting matches, and more. And earlier this year, Bumble announced it’s introducing an AI matchmaker named “Bee” to the app.

Of course, the age-related changes may not be widely felt on dating apps themselves, given most dating platforms already have 18-plus age restrictions in place. Still, many AI companion companies have a large number of teen users. Some of the most popular apps teenagers are using to connect with nonhuman companions are Character.AI, Nomi, Replika, and ChatGPT. But while ChatGPT and Claude aren’t aimed at companionship, teens are using them that way in droves. 

According to a 2025 survey from Common Sense Media, 72% of teens ages 13 to 17 have used AI companions at least once. But a staggering 52% engage with them regularly. In maybe the survey’s most telling finding, 31% said these interactions are more satisfying than talking to humans. 

Common Sense Media, a nonprofit that helps parents navigate tech and entertainment, has routinely recommended that AI companions should not be used by anyone younger than 18. In an April 2025 press release, James P. Steyer, the organization’s CEO, warned that AI companions are dangerous for minors for a host of reasons. “Social AI companions are not safe for kids. They are designed to create emotional attachment and dependency, which is particularly concerning for developing adolescent brains.”

Steyer continued: “Our testing showed these systems easily produce harmful responses, including sexual misconduct, stereotypes, and dangerous ‘advice’ that, if followed, could have life-threatening or deadly real-world impact for teens and other vulnerable people.” 

Fast Company reached out to Apple about the recent announcement but did not hear back by the time of publication.
