#10551. Beyond the Password Reset: Building Recovery Experiences That Protect Online Shopping

Have 30-200 Employees? Make $50k-$500k selling your data for AI Training.

Have 30-200 Employees? Make $50k-$500k selling your data for AI Training.

Stay up to date with AI tools, model releases, and developer workflows that matter.

An unfamiliar delivery address appears in a shopper’s account. Minutes later, an order confirmation arrives for something they never purchased. They try to sign in, but their password no longer works.

For the consumer, this is an urgent problem: stop the misuse, recover access, and understand what happened. For developers, it exposes a gap between building a login screen and building a service that remains useful when that login is compromised.

This article examines recovery from a business-to-consumer perspective: what an individual shopper needs, and how developers can translate those needs into safer interfaces and backend controls.

Account takeover and identity theft can overlap, but they are different problems.

Account takeover means someone has gained unauthorized control of an existing account. Identity theft involves misuse of someone’s personal information. Recovering access to one shopping account does not necessarily resolve misuse elsewhere.

Design the interface around questions a worried customer can answer:

A recovery page should explain the scope of help. “Recover your shopping account” is a specific promise. “Restore your identity” describes a much broader outcome that an ordinary retailer cannot deliver on its own.

Before building the workflow, list the consumer-visible assets involved: account access, addresses, order history, payment references, contact details, and support messages. Each needs its own review or remediation step.

A shopper who cannot sign in must still be able to locate help. Provide a public “My account may be compromised” entry point alongside ordinary password recovery.

Separate the two journeys. Someone who forgot a password usually needs a credential reset. Someone reporting suspicious activity may also need unauthorized changes reversed, orders investigated, and existing access revoked.

Avoid using a submitted email address as proof of ownership. A public report can initiate triage, but it should not expose order history or authorize sensitive changes.

OWASP’s Forgot Password Cheat Sheet recommends consistent responses for existing and nonexistent accounts, rate limiting, and securely generated reset tokens that expire and work only once.

If the details match an account, we’ll send instructions through an available recovery method.

The frontend message is only one part of that protection. Different response timing or API behavior can still reveal account existence.

After verifying a recovery factor, resist granting immediate access to every account feature.

A useful architecture gives the consumer a short-lived recovery session with narrowly defined permissions. For example, it might permit reviewing security settings while preventing purchases, data exports, or changes to payment information.

This type documents intent; it does not enforce security. The server must validate the session, its expiry, its association with the account, and the required permission on every request.

Check resource ownership separately. Permission to request an order review must never allow a consumer to submit another customer’s order identifier.

Do not treat an attacker’s recently changed email address as trustworthy recovery evidence. Review recovery options against previously established evidence and the account’s required level of assurance.

A new password is insufficient if an attacker still holds a valid session.

OWASP’s compromise-recovery guidance calls for reviewing recovery contacts and authentication methods, removing unauthorized changes, and invalidating existing sessions and outstanding recovery credentials after successful recovery.

For a consumer application, translate that into a visible checklist:

Use a durable workflow so a partial failure cannot silently appear as completion. Credential replacement and session revocation may span different systems; record pending work, retry failed operations safely, and show the consumer an accurate status.

JWT-based applications need particular care. Changing a password does not automatically invalidate an independently verifiable token. Choose an enforceable revocation strategy, such as checking a server-side session record or account security version on protected requests.

The OWASP Session Management Cheat Sheet provides background on session lifecycle controls.

Recovery screens are often used on a phone, in a hurry, by someone who is uncertain about what happened.

Use short steps with clear outcomes: “Review recent changes,” “Secure your sign-in,” and “Check your orders.” Explain why information is requested before asking for it.

Use native form controls with visible labels. Associate field instructions and errors with their inputs, keep keyboard navigation predictable, and move focus deliberately when a step changes. SitePoint’s HTML Form Elements guide is useful background for building these controls.

A simple reporting form might begin with:

Provide an alternative when the consumer cannot access their usual inbox. That alternative needs its own verification process; support staff should not bypass security simply because a caller sounds convincing.

Once the immediate account problem is contained, a consumer may need help addressing misuse of personal information elsewhere.

Keep this guidance separate from the application’s own recovery controls. A retailer can investigate its orders and secure its accounts. It cannot directly correct records held by unrelated organizations.

For U.S. consumers, link to the FTC’s IdentityTheft.gov as a government resource. Offer country-appropriate resources when serving other regions.

Consumers considering paid assistance can also review an identity recovery service to understand the support available for broader restoration tasks. They should check eligibility, exclusions, and service terms before relying on it.

External assistance should remain optional. Restoring access to a customer’s account should not depend on purchasing another product.

Consumers need an understandable record of what happened. Offer a case summary with relevant timestamps, reported changes, affected orders, completed actions, and unresolved questions.

Separate customer-facing information from internal investigation details. A consumer may need to know that an address changed; they do not need raw authentication tokens or internal fraud-detection rules.

Treat recovery data as sensitive. Avoid recording passwords, recovery secrets, or full payment details in logs. Restrict staff access to case information and define retention periods appropriate to its purpose.

If evidence uploads are necessary, provide a secured upload route with access controls and a deletion policy. Do not ask customers to send sensitive documents to an ordinary support inbox by default.

A successful redirect is a weak definition of recovery.

After recovery, help consumers strengthen their sign-in. SitePoint’s Developer Guide to Implementing Passkeys offers a starting point for exploring passkey authentication.

A stronger sign-in method still needs a carefully designed fallback. Evaluate the recovery path whenever you change authentication.

For a shopper, recovery succeeds when unauthorized access stops, legitimate access returns, and the next steps are clear.

Developers can support that outcome by treating recovery as a complete product journey: limited permissions, enforceable revocation, accessible interfaces, accurate case status, and clear boundaries around external assistance.

The most useful question in a design review is simple: if this were your account, could you regain control and tell what still needs attention?

#10550. Elon Musk spent nearly $500 million on the midterms. It bought him almost nothing

Elon Musk put about $474 million into the 2026 midterms, according to a New York Times tally. (That amount only tracks through October 14, when Federal Election Commission [FEC] and IRS filings stopped; the trillionaire may have given far more in dark money.) For comparison, the world’s richest man spent an estimated $250 million to get Donald Trump elected in 2024.

But this time, he has little to show for his efforts. Democrats wrested control of both the House of Representatives and Senate from Republicans Tuesday night. A Forbes analysis shows that 44 of Musk’s 106 candidates lost, including in the races that mattered most to him: Ken Paxton’s bid for a Texas Senate seat, Greg Abbott’s bid to remain Texas governor, and Vivek Ramaswamy’s bid for governor of Ohio. Eighteen Musk-backed candidates won, but all were in seats Republicans were expected to win anyway. Another 44 races remained uncalled Wednesday.

Musk’s money was funneled to Republican House and Senate candidates through his own super PAC, America PAC (about $216 million), the Senate Leadership Fund ($168 million), and the Congressional Leadership Fund for House races ($30 million).

The largest share of Musk’s midterm spending ($212 million) went toward helping Ken Paxton beat James Talarico for the Texas Senate seat formerly held by John Cornyn. Talarico walloped Paxton Tuesday night, winning by 12 points in the traditionally red state. In his victory speech, Talarico seemed to call out Musk, saying he had sent “a message to every billionaire megadonor, every trillionaire megadonor.”

Outside Texas, America PAC spent $22.7 million in six battleground states through October 20, filings show, including $8.9 million in Ohio and $7.2 million in Michigan. Democrat Sherrod Brown won the Senate seat in Ohio, while Abdul El-Sayed won the Senate seat in Michigan.

Congressional purse strings

Musk’s America PAC said its “only priority is ensuring Republicans keep full control of Washington.” His businesses rely heavily on federal money: SpaceX booked $6.78 billion in federal contracts through October 1, compared with just $3.8 billion in all of 2024, per data from federal spending tracker FedScout. In May, the U.S. Space Force awarded it $4.16 billion for Golden Dome tracking satellites. The party that controls Congress controls the government’s purse strings. Musk’s gravy train may slow down or stop.

Republicans believed Democrats would have to take Texas to seize control of Congress.

In January, Democrats will chair the committees that fund and oversee SpaceX’s biggest customers. Sen. Susan Collins (R-ME), whom America PAC backed, lost her seat—and with it, the Appropriations Committee chairmanship, which shapes NASA and Pentagon budgets.

Sen. Richard Blumenthal of Connecticut, the top Democrat on the Permanent Subcommittee on Investigations, has said he would investigate Musk and the Department of Government Efficiency (DOGE) if Democrats won. The Senate also confirms Federal Communications Commission (FCC) members, who control Starlink’s spectrum, and funds the Federal Aviation Administration (FAA), which licenses SpaceX launches. The new Congress can’t cancel contracts; the Pentagon and NASA award them.

With Paxton’s defeat, Musk also lost a reliable vote in the Senate—and gained a Texas senator in Talarico who identified him during the campaign as an out-of-touch trillionaire who personifies some of the country’s biggest problems.

Investigations

As Democrats clinched the House on Tuesday night, Rep. Robert Garcia (D-CA), who will chair the House Oversight Committee, posted two words on X: “LAWYER UP.” The warning was aimed mainly at the Trump administration and family, but Garcia’s office said he would also take on “corporate corruption,” and Musk may be at the top of that list. Democrats will run committees with subpoena power, allowing them to compel documents and testimony. In 2025, House Republicans blocked a Democratic motion to subpoena Musk. In January, Democrats will hold the gavels.

They’ve already named their targets. Committees are weighing probes of Musk’s time running DOGE, SpaceX’s and Tesla’s federal contracts, and his alleged role in restricting SpaceX’s Starshield satellite service to Ukraine’s military, Politico reports. (Musk says the U.S. military, not SpaceX, decides any limits on Starshield.)

Wall Street investors reacted quickly to Tuesday night’s election results. SpaceX shares fell 3.8% and Tesla dropped 3.5% in premarket trading on Wednesday. Overnight, Musk posted on X: “Data centers in space looking pretty appealing right now.”

What Hinojosa’s win means in Texas

Democrat Gina Hinojosa’s surprise victory over Gov. Greg Abbott could put Musk’s plans to build data centers across Texas in jeopardy. Hinojosa has proposed a moratorium on new data center construction until lawmakers enact lasting safeguards. “Data centers are coming in and doing as they please—they are guzzling up all our water, guzzling up all our electricity—and the people have no say . . . that is the Wild West of data centers that Greg Abbott has created in Texas,” she said in July.

Hinojosa wants rules giving Texas residents more say over new developments, requiring companies to prove their projects won’t raise household water or electricity bills, and prohibiting nondisclosure agreements that keep communities in the dark during the permitting process. She also wants to eliminate the government subsidies that have helped make Texas so attractive to developers.

Musk has major operations and investments in the state, including Tesla’s headquarters and largest U.S. plant, SpaceX’s Starbase launch site, and the planned Terafab semiconductor and AI chip plant. Musk gave an estimated $5.5 million to Abbott’s campaign.

Abbott’s administration gave Musk’s companies some major benefits. The governor’s office pushed broadband rules that favored Starlink, which then won about $110 million in state grants, triggering an audit. Terafab won about $1.7 billion in school tax breaks, and SpaceX more than $54 million in state grants, according to a lawsuit Hinojosa filed during the campaign.

That suit won Hinojosa access to more than 1,000 pages of Abbott-Musk communications that Abbott had called too “intimate and embarrassing” to release. In one message, Musk asked whether Abbott would “have his back,” to which Abbott replied, “100%.”

When she takes office in January, Hinojosa will control future incentive deals. She’ll also appoint the Texas Parks commissioners who would vote on any sale of Boca Chica State Park, which Musk wants to buy to expand SpaceX’s Starbase rocket facility in South Texas.

What the losses cost Musk

The $224 million Musk spent and lost in Texas isn’t likely to hurt his wallet much. He’s worth about $902 billion today, so he lost roughly one-fortieth of 1% of his wealth.

But the loss of a friendly Congress—and the diminished political clout of Musk’s friend Trump—could cost much more. About one-fifth of SpaceX’s $18.7 billion in 2025 revenue came from federal agencies, its initial public offering (IPO) filing says. That’s roughly $3.7 billion a year, or $7.5 billion over two years at 2025 levels. The Democratic Congress could decide to slow-walk new contracts, like May’s $4.16 billion Golden Dome award.

Musk now pitches SpaceX as a supplier of AI computing. Deals renting its Colossus data centers to Anthropic and Google could bring in $26 billion a year. The changing political tide could make getting permits for new data centers more difficult. In August, even the Musk-friendly Abbott paused new data center connections to the Texas grid.

The election results could also shake investors’ confidence in Musk and the companies he leads. SpaceX’s IPO filing calls the company “highly dependent” on Musk. When investors buy SpaceX or Tesla stock, they’re not just looking at the companies’ financials; they’re also buying into the “story” of Musk, who has fashioned an image of an unpredictable engineering genius with massive wealth and powerful friends. But his political connections look considerably less secure after Tuesday night. That could make investors less inclined to believe Musk’s claims that SpaceX will put data centers in space and become the largest AI company in the world.

On Tuesday morning, Musk tweeted “Vote red today!” But by Wednesday morning, the tweet had quietly disappeared.

#10548. Canva’s big layoffs say a lot about the AI design landscape

The AI design giant Canva just announced the first-ever major round of layoffs in its 13-year history. As part of the restructuring, 1,271 people—around 22% of the company’s overall staff—will either be laid off, reassigned to new roles, or relocated to the company’s headquarters in Sydney, Australia. 

News of the layoffs was announced on November 3 (a perfect day to bury some bad news) in a press release from Canva cofounder and CEO Melanie Perkins. In the note, Perkins explains that the layoffs are part of a larger plan to make Canva’s teams more agile and less siloed, including by folding product, growth, and platform teams into one unit and reducing the number of “subspecialities” at the company.

“I’ve come to the difficult conclusion that small changes won’t be enough,” Perkin’s letter reads. “To set ourselves up for the next decade, we need to refound Canva, getting back to our roots of small, empowered teams with the freedom to make decisions, take ownership and focus on what matters most for our community.”

While Canva didn’t provide a broader business reason for the layoffs, the restructuring comes at a time when it’s working through some mounting growing pains and questions about the timing of a potential IPO. After spending the last several years going all-in on its AI-powered product suite, Canva is now facing the challenge of squaring its business model with an increasingly voracious user base.

Canva’s growth conundrum

In May, Fast Company wrote that design was entering its “frenemies” era. 

At the time, Anthropic had just launched Claude Design. The product seemingly came as a surprise to incumbent companies including Adobe and Figma, which had been operating under a multiyear collaboration with Anthropic to integrate Claude into their products, and didn’t expect the AI giant to debut its own design competitor. Meanwhile, Canva told Fast Company that it had actually helped Anthropic develop Claude Design, despite Canva’s own collaboration deal with the company. 

For Adobe, Figma, and Canva, working with frontier models offers the advantage of bringing new tools to market faster and benefiting from the sophistication of frontier models. The main downside is that using these frontier models also takes a lot of computing power, and that racks up major costs. As Canva has made a major push—by building its own models and acquiring AI companies—to become an “AI platform” over the last several years, those costs have become a significant problem.

In early August, Canva sent a note to its investors with an update: the company was downgrading its revenue growth forecast for 2026 from 30% to 20%. At the time, Perkins told shareholders that the “average cost of serving an AI task was too high” as the company relied heavily on its partnerships with frontier models to complete users’ requests. 

For context, by the end of 2025, Canva had more than 265 million monthly active users and more than 31 million paid users, meaning that some large portion of AI traffic on the site was likely generated by free users. In an August interview with Fortune, Perkins said that users’ demand for new AI features had “significantly exceeded” the company’s expectations, which came with both pros and cons. 

“This validated the demand, but also showed us we needed to reduce the cost of completing an AI task to support a broad rollout,” Perkins told the publication. “Rather than broadly rolling out a product before the underlying economics were ready, we decided to slow the rollout while we rebuilt the architecture, reduced unit costs and strengthened the business model.”

To reduce the intermediary costs that Canva incurs every time an AI task requires a frontier model, Canva has been working on developing first-party tools that can take up some of the work. For example, Perkins told Fortune that, since launching Canva 2.0 in April, the company’s cost-per-task has reduced by 90%. This October, Canva launched another product called Canva Brush, which it said reduced cost-per-task by 46% compared to the previous design agent. 

These new features have made improvements, but, based on its downgraded revenue forecast, Canva still has a ways to go before it fully irons out its economic model. The fact that user demand for Canva’s AI tools is outpacing its own capabilities seems to be a bullish sign for AI design at large. Now, Canva needs to figure out how to make the most of the surge—and the company’s first major layoffs could be part of its plan to get back on track.

#10546. McDonald’s to add new value bundles next year

McDonald’s plans to introduce new value-oriented meal bundles early next year after a disappointing third quarter that saw lower traffic at U.S. restaurants.

McDonald’s Chairman and CEO Chris Kempczinski said Wednesday that the company recently began an eight-week test of mix-and-match and fixed-price bundles at 1,900 U.S. restaurants. Those bundles might feature a McChicken sandwich and small fries for $3.50, for example.

But around 4,000 franchisees have decided not to wait for the test results and have launched meal bundles of their own, he said.

“Customers should see a clear and compelling value proposition every time they consider McDonald’s, whether they’re looking for an affordable individual item, a complete meal, or a digital offer in the mobile app,” Kempczinski said during a conference call with investors.

U.S. same-store sales—or sales at locations open at least a year—fell 0.2% in the July-September period, the Chicago burger giant said Wednesday. While that was not as bad as the 0.5% drop Wall Street had expected, it was the first retreat for McDonald’s since early 2025.

McDonald’s restored some regional and national in-app deals and shifted some marketing spending to support value meals, which helped push same-store sales into positive territory in September and October. But the shift in focus at McDonald’s shows how challenging the economic environment has become for U.S. fast-food companies, which are losing customers as many Americans struggle with higher gas prices and the uncomfortably high cost of living.

Third-quarter foot traffic fell 2.6% across the entire fast-food sector in the U.S., according to Revenue Management Solutions, a restaurant industry consultant.

McDonald’s has been tweaking its U.S. value offerings for more than two years to try to lure back lower-income customers and better compete with rivals like Taco Bell, which offers a menu of 10 items that each cost $3 or less.

In June 2024, McDonald’s introduced a $5 Meal Deal. The next year, it debuted its McValue menu and Extra Value Meals, which promise a 15% discount for a bundled meal compared with buying items individually. In April, it revamped the McValue menu, adding 10 items that cost $3 or less.

But not all of McDonald’s franchisees—who own 95% of the company’s U.S. restaurants—have been on board. Kempczinski said in August that only 60% of its U.S. restaurants were offering the revamped McValue menu. McDonald’s replaced its U.S. president that same month.

Kempczinski said the company’s previous efforts haven’t been enough because they didn’t offer compelling low-end deals. “You need to have good entry-level value, particularly with the low-income consumer,” he said.

Globally, same-store sales rose 1.3% in the third quarter. Strong sales in Germany and Australia helped offset weakness in France, which was rocked by protests that began in September.

Revenue rose 1% to $7.16 billion for the quarter, short of Wall Street expectations of $7.28 billion.

Net income rose 9% to $2.49 billion. Adjusted for onetime items, the company earned $3.57 per share. That beat analysts’ forecast for a $3.38 per-share profit.

Shares rose more than 5% in morning trading Wednesday.

—By Dee-Ann Durbin, AP business writer

#10545. Top 5 3D Animation Software in 2026

Have 30-200 Employees? Make $50k-$500k selling your data for AI Training.

Have 30-200 Employees? Make $50k-$500k selling your data for AI Training.

Stay up to date with AI tools, model releases, and developer workflows that matter.

Choosing the best 3D animation software depends on your experience, budget, and creative goals. Some tools offer complete 3D modeling and animation workflows, while others specialize in professional character animation, visual effects, or AI-powered video creation. This guide compares five options and notes how each fits into web and game projects, so designers and developers can see which one suits their pipeline.

Blender is one of the strongest free options for anyone looking for comprehensive 3D animation software. This open-source application combines modeling, sculpting, rigging, animation, rendering, simulation, and compositing in one package.

Blender provides a broad production workflow without requiring users to pay for a standard commercial license. Its active community, learning resources, and add-on ecosystem make it accessible to independent creators. It is suitable for everything from simple animated scenes to complex short films and game assets.

For web and game developers: Blender ships with a glTF 2.0 importer and exporter, and glTF is the format libraries such as three.js load for 3D on the web. See the Blender manual’s glTF page for export options.

Its extensive interface and feature set can feel overwhelming to new users. Learning advanced rigging, lighting, materials, and rendering takes time, and some established studios may have specialized pipelines built around other applications.

Beginners, freelancers, indie game developers, students, and professionals who need a powerful 3D animation tool without a software subscription.

Autodesk Maya is a professional 3D application widely associated with character animation, rigging, film production, and game development. It offers detailed control over character movement and complex animation workflows, making it a strong choice for artists working in established production environments.

Maya provides sophisticated tools for animating characters and managing complex scenes. Its established role in many professional workflows makes it a valuable skill for artists pursuing careers in film, television, and game development. It also offers detailed control over animation timing, character motion, and rig behavior.

Maya generally requires a paid subscription, which can be expensive for hobbyists and independent creators. Its advanced interface also takes time to learn, particularly for users who have never worked with professional 3D software.

Professional animators, film and television artists, game studios, and users who need advanced character animation and rigging capabilities.

Cinema 4D is a 3D modeling, animation, and rendering application known for its motion graphics workflow. It is widely used for commercial visuals, broadcast graphics, product animations, and creative work that combines 3D elements with graphic design.

Cinema 4D is a strong option for designers who want to create polished motion graphics and branded animation. Its MoGraph workflow can make repetitive or complex movements easier to manage, and its integration with common design workflows is helpful for agencies and creative teams.

For web and product designers: Cinema 4D includes a glTF exporter, which helps when a designer needs to hand a 3D model to a developer for the web. Maxon documents the options on its glTF export settings page.

Cinema 4D is a commercial product, so ongoing licensing costs may be a concern. Although it can handle a wide range of 3D work, users focused on highly specialized character animation or procedural visual effects may prefer tools designed around those workflows.

Motion designers, advertising agencies, broadcast artists, product visualization specialists, and creators who regularly produce animated graphics.

Houdini, developed by SideFX, is a 3D software package known for procedural workflows and advanced visual effects. Rather than relying entirely on manually created steps, artists can build systems that generate and modify complex scenes, simulations, and effects.

Houdini offers exceptional flexibility for technical artists and visual-effects specialists. Procedural workflows make it possible to create reusable systems and adjust complex effects efficiently. Its capabilities are particularly valuable when a project needs detailed simulations or large numbers of interconnected elements.

For game developers: SideFX offers Houdini Engine plugins for Unity and Unreal Engine, which let procedural Houdini assets be used inside those engines. SideFX explains the plugins in its Houdini Engine FAQ.

Houdini has a steep learning curve, especially for beginners who are unfamiliar with node-based workflows. Building effective procedural systems requires patience and technical understanding. While free learning options are available, some commercial uses and advanced workflows require an appropriate paid license.

Visual-effects artists, technical directors, simulation specialists, and experienced 3D creators working on demanding film, television, or game projects.

MagicLight.AI is different from the four tools above. It is an AI-powered video creation platform rather than a traditional 3D application, so it produces finished animated videos, not editable 3D scenes, rigs, or game assets. It is included here for readers who want animated storytelling without building a 3D pipeline. It supports AI-generated characters, scene creation, storyboarding, and voice features.

MagicLight.AI can reduce the time and technical effort needed to create animated videos. It is particularly useful for content creators, educators, marketers, and storytellers who want to focus on the script and final message rather than mastering a complex 3D production pipeline.

MagicLight.AI is not a replacement for dedicated 3D software when you need precise control over mesh topology, character rigs, keyframes, physics, or custom 3D scenes. Creators who need editable 3D assets for games or studio production will need a conventional 3D application such as the ones above.

Content creators, educators, and marketers who want to produce animated videos efficiently without learning a traditional 3D animation workflow.

The right software is the one that supports your actual production needs. Before choosing a tool, consider the following factors.

If you want to model objects, build character rigs, and control animation precisely, start with a dedicated 3D application such as Blender or Maya. If your goal is to create animated storytelling videos from scripts or ideas with less manual production work, an AI video tool such as MagicLight.AI may be a more convenient option.

Blender is an excellent starting point if you need a complete 3D toolset without a standard license fee. Houdini also has a free Apprentice edition with restrictions. Maya and Cinema 4D are commercial applications, so compare their current plans against your expected usage before committing.

Different applications suit different workflows. Blender is versatile, Maya excels at character animation, Cinema 4D is well suited to motion graphics, and Houdini is especially powerful for procedural effects. MagicLight.AI is better suited to AI-assisted video production than to detailed, manually controlled 3D scene creation.

Beginners may find Blender’s extensive learning resources helpful, although its broad feature set takes time to master. Maya and Houdini demand more specialized skills for advanced work, while Cinema 4D is often considered by motion designers seeking a more direct design-oriented workflow. AI video tools can reduce the amount of technical setup required, but still require creative direction and review.

Think about where the finished animation will be used. A web project may need a lightweight glTF model. A game project may require exportable 3D assets, rig compatibility, and a game-engine workflow. A commercial motion graphic may depend on rendering and compositing integration. A social video or animated explainer may prioritize turnaround time, narration, subtitles, and scene continuity.

The best 3D animation software in 2026 depends on your budget, experience, and intended output. Blender is the strongest starting point for many users who want a comprehensive free 3D workflow. Autodesk Maya is a compelling option for professional character animation, Cinema 4D suits motion graphics and commercial visuals, and Houdini stands out for procedural effects and complex simulations. MagicLight.AI offers a different approach: it helps creators generate animated videos with AI rather than manually building a traditional 3D production pipeline.

Blender is one of the best free options because it includes modeling, rigging, animation, rendering, and other production tools in a single open-source application. It is suitable for beginners as well as experienced artists.

Yes. Free software can support professional-quality work when used effectively. Blender, for example, provides a comprehensive toolset for animation and rendering. The final result depends on the artist’s skills, project requirements, hardware, and production workflow.

Blender is a strong choice for beginners who want to learn traditional 3D modeling and animation without paying for a standard software license. Those who mainly want to create animated videos from stories or scripts may prefer exploring an AI video creation platform such as MagicLight.AI.

Blender and Cinema 4D can both export glTF, a format widely used for 3D on the web. Blender is free, so it is the easiest place to start.

#10543. This map shows just how big Democrats won the midterms

The 2026 election was a total political reset from 2024, with many states that voted for President Donald Trump last time swinging to the left and giving Democrats control of the next Congress. A pair of maps shows through arrows just how dramatic the change in just two years really was.

To communicate the shift in vote margin from one party to another from the most two recent elections, The New York Times has used an election results map with arrows that show the shift in each individual county where most votes are now counted. Blue arrows to the left show a trend towards Democrats compared to the last election while red arrows to the right show a trend towards Republicans. The longer the arrow, the bigger the shift. Two years ago, that map was covered in red. It’s now filled by a sea of blue arrows.

The Times first use the arrows map 10 years ago to show the vote shift in 2016, and Times graphics editor Wilson Andrews told Fast Company in 2024 the style “adds another layer of storytelling.” While typical election map graphics show you the winner or vote share, this map conveys a sense of time, giving viewers a look at how much political attitudes changed from one Election Day to another.

Trump won the national popular vote in 2024 after making campaign promises to lower prices and avoid foreign wars, but in office he did the opposite, by illegally imposing tariffs and launching a war with Iran. These policy decisions raised costs, as did broad government corruption, pet construction projects that cost hundreds of millions of dollars, and his administration’s overly aggressive immigration enforcement tactics, which flipped many Latino voters he’d won in the previous election cycle.

In just two years, Trump’s positive approval rating dropped near its lowest ever—and is the lowest net approval rating for any incumbent president in a midterm since polling began. Tuesday’s results shows what that means from county to county in stark terms.

The Times shift map is an especially compelling piece of data visualization to depict upsets, because it subverts what we’re used to seeing from standard red-blue election results maps. Instead of just “red states” and “blue states,” that show you the winner, it shows where in the country the vote has most swung. The 2026 map shows tiny blue arrows in Democratic strongholds like Oregon, because the vote margin shift wasn’t that great, while in places we’re used to seeing always colored in red, like Texas or Kansas, the longest blue arrows blanket the state.

Democratic House Leader Hakeem Jeffries called Tuesday a “change election,” and Democrats pulled off wins Tuesday in historically Republican places: Annie Andrews became the first Democrat to win a U.S. Senate seat in South Carolina since 1998, James Talarico became the first in Texas since 1988, and Adam Hamilton became the first in Kansas since 1932. Branding themselves as centrists, these Democrats ran in an especially unfavorable year for Republicans tied to an unpopular president that many of them didn’t even want to mention.

Showing election results through the shift in margin has become a popular form of data viz, and other outlets like The Economist and NBC News did their own versions of the map this year too. The story of U.S. midterms is one of buyers’ remorse, and long blue arrows in deep red states quickly show just how forcefully much of the American electorate wanted a refund.

#10541. Red wasn’t always Republican. The surprising history behind America’s political color divide

“Better dead than red.”

Cold War conservatives used to say that, and they meant it: Better to suffer nuclear annihilation, they believed, than endure a “red” victory. And by “red” they meant anyone on the left of the political spectrum—from the Soviet communists to their “fellow travelers” in the U.S.

It’s strange, then, that America’s conservative party, the Republican Party, is now the red one. There’s no ideology behind the switch, no founding decision by either party to claim a color as its own. The whole red-state/blue-state vocabulary is much newer than most people assume. It dates almost exactly from the 2000 election.

And in many cases, it fails to capture the reality of politics in America.

When nobody could agree on a color scheme

Television networks needed to distinguish two candidates on a map, and for decades they just picked whatever looked good that year.

In 1976, NBC colored GOP presidential candidate Gerald Ford’s states blue and Democrat Jimmy Carter’s states red. Four years later, that same scheme meant Republican presidential candidate Ronald Reagan’s landslide victory painted the map almost entirely blue, which is a strange thing to picture now, given how thoroughly Reagan became the patron saint of the red party.

That wasn’t just a one-network quirk, either. The Washington Post was still assigning red to Democrats and blue to Republicans in graphics used during the 2000 campaign.

If you go looking for the decision that gave American politics its colors, you won’t find one. You’ll find almost a quarter-century in which nobody had settled on today’s version.

Bush v. Gore

That inconsistency ended in 2000 with the fight over Florida’s presidential votes, though nobody at any TV network decided it should.

The networks covering the presidential contest between Republican George W. Bush and Democrat—and sitting Vice President—Al Gore happened, that year, to converge on red for Bush and blue for Gore. NBC’s Tim Russert is often credited with popularizing the phrase “red states” during the campaign, though the exact origin is disputed.

Under normal circumstances, none of this would have mattered much. Four years later, some other combination might have taken hold, the way it always had before.

But 2000 wasn’t normal.

The election stayed unresolved for five weeks while Florida’s votes were counted, contested in court and counted again. Night after night, on every channel, Americans watched the same map, colored the same way.

By the time the U.S. Supreme Court ended it and Bush was certified the winner by 537 votes, the color scheme – red for Republican Bush and blue for Democrat Gore – had become familiar enough to stop looking like a choice at all. Nobody argued anyone into it; the map just stayed in front of the country long enough to seem inevitable.

The labels started doing more work

Once red and blue attached themselves to the parties, they didn’t stay confined to maps.

By the 2002 midterms, journalists were already writing about “two Americas: red and blue,” as though the country had sorted itself into two coherent cultures overnight.

By the 2004 campaign, the vocabulary was everywhere, carrying connotations that nobody had assigned it on purpose. Red became associated with rural America, religiosity, the South and the interior West; blue with cities, more secular electorates, the coasts and college towns.

There’s truth buried in that shorthand: American political geography really has sorted itself along those lines – more than it used to, at least.

But the language hardened fast, turning a graphics convention into shorthand for identities it was never built to describe. Within a couple of election cycles, pundits were talking about red America and blue America as though they were two different countries with two different sets of values, rather than two loose clusters of states that happen to vote differently.

The 2000 contested presidential election cemented the red-blue America convention.

What the map doesn’t show

I’m a political scientist, and here’s the problem I see with this crude way of presenting voter preferences. A state decided by 2 percentage points gets colored exactly the same solid shade as a state decided by 30. Pennsylvania in a close year and Wyoming in a landslide show up looking identical, even though one of them is split down the middle.

The map doesn’t lie about who won – it just can’t show you how close it was. The result, after 20-some years of maps built that way, is a picture of the country that looks more neatly sorted than the electorate actually is.

The red-blue convention didn’t invent regional political differences. Those are real, and they’ve been growing for decades.

What the convention does is magnify them. A standard election map colors each state by who carried it, not by the margin – a state won by 4 points gets the same solid shade as one won by 26. That’s not a limit of the medium; color could run on a gradient just as easily. It’s a choice, and one that tracks the actual mechanics of the election: The Electoral College is winner-take-all, so a map showing only the winner in each state is reproducing the same either/or logic that decides who gets the electoral votes.

A third color exists for exactly this problem. Princeton’s Robert Vanderbei built the first “Purple America” map after the 2000 election, shading each county somewhere between true blue and true red according to its vote split. Landslide counties are rare, so most of the map came out some shade of purple. The technique got wider attention after 2004 – Vanderbei’s map was Newsweek’s “click of the day” on its website, though it never ran in the magazine itself – and others built their own versions afterward.

But purple never became the convention. It turns up in academic work and the occasional data-journalism piece built to correct a flatter map – but rarely on the graphic behind a network anchor, and almost never in a candidate’s own description of the country.

By the time anyone offered the correction, red and blue were no longer just colors on a map. They were the language.

A reputation never quite earned

America’s conservative party ending up red is a decent trivia fact, the kind of thing that makes for good conversation at dinner. The real oddity runs deeper than that irony, though.

An arbitrary graphics convention, repeated for five weeks during a contested recount, hardened into a vocabulary that Americans now use to describe political geography, culture, and identity, as if the country had always divided itself this cleanly into two camps.

It never did.

Andrew Latham is a professor of political science at Macalester College.

#10540. ‘I am standing on shoulders made of steel’: Keisha Lance Bottoms highlights Georgia’s fraught history in rousing victory speech

Former Atlanta Mayor Keisha Lance Bottoms has been elected governor of Georgia, making her the first Black woman in the U.S. to hold the position. She also used her victory speech as a platform to highlight just how far the state has come.

In her speech on the night of November 3 in Atlanta, Bottoms opened up about her family’s past, referencing her family members Shephard and Betsy Peek, who were enslaved in Crawfordsville during the mid-1800s.

Bottoms shared how the day prior to the election, she visited the same town that her relatives once called home, with the trip becoming its own revelation for the Democrat.

“I visited the grave of Betsy Peak, my great-great grandmother, who was born in 1845, 30 years before emancipation,” she said. “In a cemetery field filled with unmarked graves, I found hers.”

She added, “I don’t know what dreams Betsy Peak had for her children or for her grandchildren or the generations that she would never meet, but I know I am standing on shoulders made of steel.”

But the same town—home to at least five generations of her family—was also home to a very different chapter of Georgia’s history.

“It was the town that was home to the former governor of Georgia and the vice president of the Confederate States of America, Alexander Stephens,” she said.

“Georgia is not defined by one moment in time”

The emotive speech and Bottoms’s historic win come more than 100 years after the Emancipation Proclamation and the Confederacy, with the governor-elect set to lead the state where her own family members were once enslaved.

She added, “yes, Crawfordsville produced the Confederacy’s vice president, but tonight it also produced your next governor.”

But the irony was not lost on her, turning the story into a lesson.

She added, “tonight should remind as that no matter what community we come from, Georgia is not defined by one moment in time or by one person—it’s been defined by all of us.”

You can watch the full speech on C-SPAN.

#10536. ‘I don’t feel like libbing out’: LGBTQ+ rights took blows in these states despite midterm election blue wave

For Democrats, this week’s midterm elections went nearly as well as they could have hoped. The party has gained at least seven seats in the Senate and 29 in the House of Representatives, securing full Congressional control for Democrats. Some conservative strongholds even flipped blue, including Texas, Kansas, and South Carolina.

The election also marked a number of groundbreaking firsts for the country, including the first Black woman to serve as governor, the first openly gay man elected to the Senate, and the first Muslim elected to the Senate. 

But the so-called “blue tsunami” doesn’t mean liberal policies won out everywhere, even in places where Democrats gained or maintained control. Four states passed or are close to passing ballot initiatives to restrict the rights of transgender children, including three that voted blue in this election.

States’ anti-trans initiatives

So far, two ballot initiatives restricting the rights of trans student athletes have already passed. That includes Nebraska’s Initiative 442, which amends the state’s constitution to require that schools designate sports teams as male, female, or coeducational based on “biological sex,” also banning “students of the male sex” from playing on girls’ teams. The measure passed with 68% approval.

Also already passed is Arizona’s Proposition 318, which similarly requires schools to designate teams by gender and prohibit any students assigned male at birth from playing on girls’ teams. Unlike Nebraska, Arizona was solidly blue in this election, with Democratic Governor Katie Hobbs winning reelection.

The other states with initiatives about trans athletes on their ballots include Colorado and Washington, both of which have Democratic governors and two Democratic senators.

In Colorado, two ballot initiatives centered on trans children. Proposition 134 would follow Arizona and Nebraska’s lead in requiring athletes to play on teams matching their sex assigned at birth, while Proposition 135 would prohibit gender-affirming surgery for minors.

Washington’s Initiative 638 is perhaps the most controversial of all these measures. Beyond banning students from playing on sports teams not matching their sex assigned at birth, the initiative would also require that all players on girls’ teams provide a statement from a medical provider verifying their sex, potentially through genital exams.

Colorado and Washington’s measures are still too close to call, but reports show they are currently on track for approval.

LGBTQ+ social media reacts

Amid online celebration in the wake of the blue tsunami, the success of these anti-trans measures has spoiled for some what would otherwise be a resounding political victory.

“I don’t feel like ‘libbing out,’” reads one viral post sharing a graphic of the initiatives’ early results. It’s garnered more than 243,000 views on X.

“Yes, there is a blue wave. but the amount of transphobic initiatives are passing, even in deep blue states, is very very concerning,” wrote another user.

Others agreed that the measures’ success in Democratic strongholds was especially troublesome: “‘Blue wave’ but trans people aren’t even safe in Denver, Colorado,” reads one response to the news.

“Blue wave is great but please don’t leave trans women and girls behind while you celebrate,” asked a fourth user. “Trans girl’s rights were successfully taken away yesterday in several states, they’re still here and deserve to be fought for.”

#10534. Exposed to PHP2Shell? Cyber Experts Weigh in With Advice

Fixing the critical PHP flaws is not as simple as clicking "Update." Here's how to assess your risk, and what you can do to protect yourself.

New data shows that organizations aren't moving to patch PHP2Shell as fast as attackers are moving to exploit it. It's understandable, cybersecurity experts say, because updating in this case is especially complicated.

The data began trickling in on Oct. 21, painting a picture of the world's initial response to the new PHP vulnerabilities. The picture wasn't pretty.

Some well-positioned experts picked up on a remarkable volume of threat activity. Cloudflare CEO Matthew Prince stated that in the 10 hours before the vulnerabilities were publicly disclosed on Oct. 21, his company observed thousands of exploitation attempts. "That jumped to tens of thousands in the 45 minutes post announcement, hundreds of thousands within 2 hours, and millions now," he wrote on X, late on Oct. 21.

The next day, Check Point Research claimed that attempts at exploitation had already reached 10% of organizations worldwide. On the flip side, only a small percentage of vulnerable organizations have been visibly updating to new PHP releases.

Related:Critical Rails Bug Threatens to Derail Vulnerable Servers

Using discoverable deployments on Shodan as a sample, Ox Security researchers found that more than 99% of instances were not yet advertising a newly patched version 24 hours after fixed versions were made available. Researchers at Flare piled on, noting that 73% of those instances advertised PHP branches that no longer receive updates from the PHP Foundation. (It also qualified these figures, noting that basic Internet scanning misses some crucial nuances.)

Meanwhile, Cisco Talos estimated, based on open source intelligence (OSINT), that around half of all PHP systems won't receive patches.

On the morning of Oct. 23, Eastern time, Ox informed Dark Reading that its 99% figure had dropped to 97.5%. And Flare told Dark Reading that of the 27% of public records reflecting upstream-supported branches, about 5% have been updated.

Addressing PHP2Shell is often not as simple as clicking "Update," practitioners acknowledge. Still, there are steps that most organizations can take to protect themselves immediately, like diligently looking for PHP deployments across an organization's entire fleet of systems, hunting for signs of compromise, and restricting access to or otherwise taking offline any systems that can't be patched immediately.

In principle, protecting against PHP2Shell should be simple. There are new versions one can update to, which cover the vulnerabilities in question, CVE-2026-109618 and CVE-2026-109619. In practice, addressing PHP2Shell will look very different from one organization to the next, and require more or less effort, depending on how, where, and in what ways they use PHP.

Related:Undead Software Projects Continue to Raise Security Risks

The unanimous first step all cybersecurity experts point to is that organizations should discover and inventory all of the assets they have running PHP. It's easier said than done. As the Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency (CISA) noted in an Oct. 21 security alert, PHP isn't just something that runs websites; it's "often a component of other software and prevalence may not be directly observable."

Flare researchers saw that firsthand when examining the attack surface. "What stood out to me during the research was how much PHP we found outside conventional web hosting," says Adrian Cheek, senior cybercrime researcher at Flare. "We identified it in storage devices, physical access-control systems, cameras and remote-access interfaces. If you're only looking at your main websites or limiting an external assessment to ports 80 and 443, you're going to miss some of that."

For organizations with this sort of exposure, he continues, "You generally can't log into a storage appliance or physical access-control unit and independently upgrade its PHP installation. You need the manufacturer to provide updated firmware. If the manufacturer has stopped supporting that product, the organization may have no patch available."

Related:Claude Model Builds Exploits Across Major Browsers & OSes

Putting edge cases aside, let's assume that an organization has managed to find and list out all of its PHP deployments. From there, remarkably, things only get more complicated.

Publicly available data seems to suggest that most PHP out in the world is running on old branches. "If you’re running an application built around PHP 5 or PHP 7, moving to a current PHP release could mean rewriting parts of the application, replacing dependencies, and testing everything that might break. There’s a good reason why organizations avoid doing that casually, particularly when the application supports something operationally important," Cheek explains.

In these cases, remediation will be a slow process, if organizations choose to pursue it at all. Luckily, and confusingly, old PHP versions aren't always unsavable.

The most common version in public records, 7.4.3, is what shipped with Ubuntu 20.04. As Cheek points out, "Linux distributions frequently retain an older PHP version number while backporting security fixes. So an old version number doesn't automatically mean the software hasn't been patched." Besides operating systems, applications can also backport fixes for the PHP they come packaged with.

Thus, organizations running outdated PHP actually fall into very distinct buckets: Some organizations will need to do the heavy lifting necessary to migrate or replace their applications or products. In the meantime, experts say, they should consider taking their vulnerable systems offline entirely. Cheek also offers one pro tip to mitigate CVE-2026-109619, for those that can reach the PHP configuration.

"The reported attacks run through PHP session upload progress, a feature that is on by default and needs no session_start call in the application. Disabling session.upload_progress.enabled and restarting the PHP workers blocks the confirmed session-upload-progress attack paths without requiring a PHP version upgrade," he explains, with the qualification that it doesn't address the other PHP2Shell flaw, CVE-2026-109618, so it's a temporary measure at best.

Some organizations will be privileged enough to install backported fixes through their vendors. On Oct. 21, Ubuntu developer Canonical published fixes for PHP2Shell for all versions since 14.04. Even these relieved parties will have more accounting work to do, since an OS or application update doesn't necessarily carry a full PHP version upgrade. If one takes advantage of Ubuntu's updates, future scans could continue to show it ostensibly running PHP 7.4.3.

And don't forget, Cheek says: "The restart matters. Installing a corrected PHP package doesn't necessarily replace the interpreter already loaded into running worker processes."

Besides all of the technical details, size will determine a lot about how organizations can respond to PHP2Shell.

As with any urgent cybersecurity vulnerability, small businesses may start off with disadvantages in awareness as well as the resources needed to get themselves cleaned up. Yet after 48 hours of working nonstop to help more than 1,000 organizations with PHP2Shell, OX Security CEO Neatsun Ziv is quicker to point out the advantages in being small. "

At small organizations, you can do whatever you want. You just go in and patch. You wait five hours. Nobody complains about breaking anything," he says.

But larger organizations are different, he says. "They've got a golden image — one server baseline they update," Ziv says. "It's always a downstream model: you deploy a new golden image, this golden image is then being built with new software, this new software goes to production, and nobody can change production. This is the norm in deployments today. Nobody goes to servers and actually patches them. It just becomes unmaintainable in the long term."

And that's to say nothing of just how many people from different teams need to be involved in major updates within a large organization; or of how major organizations run disproportionately significant systems that can't afford to break; or of how prevalent and varied PHP can be even within organizations. As Ziv notes, "Most of the organizations that we work with found hundreds of servers that are running PHP."

Check Point chief security and trust officer Alex Spokoiny adds that even beyond one's own house, organizations also face risk from how all of their suppliers handle PHP2Shell.

"The first step is to engage the relevant suppliers and understand how they are responding. Are they affected? What protections have they put in place? When do they expect remediation to be completed? If you cannot get clear or reasonable answers to those questions, that is itself something you need to factor into your risk assessment and potentially consider alternative options," he advises.

Organizations can also team up, to everyone's benefit. "For example, where technically possible, they may be able to extend their own Web application firewall (WAF) protection to applications operated by third parties, helping reduce exposure while the provider works toward a permanent fix," Spokoiny says.

Nate Nelson is a journalist and award-winning scriptwriter. In addition to Dark Reading he writes for Darknet Diaries, the most popular show in cybersecurity across all media.

He began his career as a freelancer, ghostwriting Forbes and CNBC op-eds for executives in tech and finance. Then he transitioned to journalism at Threatpost, where he covered cybersecurity news and trends. Throughout those years he co-created a cybersecurity podcast, Malicious Life, which in its day climbed into the Top 20 technology podcasts charts on Apple Podcasts and Spotify.

He holds degrees from New York University and Bard College. As a born and bred New Yorker, he enjoys a superiority complex, but is polite enough to keep it to himself.

#10533. How to Test Location-Aware APIs with FastAPI and PostGIS

Have 30-200 Employees? Make $50k-$500k selling your data for AI Training.

Have 30-200 Employees? Make $50k-$500k selling your data for AI Training.

Stay up to date with AI tools, model releases, and developer workflows that matter.

Catch coordinate-order bugs, distance mistakes, boundary cases, and bad spatial assumptions before they reach production.

A location endpoint can return HTTP 200 and still be wrong by kilometers. That is the uncomfortable part of testing geospatial APIs: ordinary API checks tell you whether the request worked, not whether the geography is correct.

Spatial bugs can look harmless in code review. Latitude and longitude get reversed. A radius value is treated as degrees instead of meters. A query works near one city but behaves differently elsewhere because the geometry column uses the wrong type. The JSON is valid, the tests are green, and the map is still wrong.

In this tutorial, you will build a small FastAPI endpoint backed by PostGIS and then test the spatial behavior directly. The examples use deterministic fixtures positioned at known distances, so the tests verify geography rather than only response structure.

The API exposes one endpoint: GET /places/nearby. A client sends longitude, latitude, and a radius in meters. The service returns nearby places as GeoJSON features, ordered by distance.

The useful part is not the endpoint itself. The useful part is the test strategy. We will check coordinate validation, exact distance boundaries, GeoJSON coordinate order, and the database query that turns a radius into a spatial filter.

Use a geography column when the API is answering human-scale distance questions in meters. PostGIS can then calculate on the ellipsoid instead of treating longitude and latitude as flat Cartesian coordinates.

The endpoint below validates longitude, latitude, and radius with Pydantic, then sends a parameterized query to PostgreSQL. The SQL uses ST_DWithin to filter candidates and ST_Distance to return the measured distance.

The API accepts lon and lat as separate named parameters. That removes ambiguity at the HTTP boundary. GeoJSON still uses [longitude, latitude] when the response is created.

Hard-coding two real businesses and hoping their distance is approximately right makes a fragile test. A better approach is to create test points at exact distances from a fixed origin.

PostGIS can generate those fixtures with ST_Project. In the test database, create one point 500 meters away, one 950 meters away, and one 1,500 meters away. Now a 1,000-meter query has an unambiguous expected result: the first two belong in the response and the third does not.

This is the first test that actually proves something spatial. It is not checking that the endpoint returns a list. It is checking that the 1-kilometer contract means what the API says it means.

GeoJSON coordinates are longitude first, latitude second. Many developers naturally think latitude first because that is how coordinates are commonly spoken. A validation layer can catch the most obvious reversal before the database ever sees it.

Longitude must be between -180 and 180. Latitude must be between -90 and 90. That will not catch every reversal, because both numbers may sometimes fall inside both ranges, but it catches a large class of failures and gives clients a useful error instead of a misleading map.

A response can be syntactically valid JSON and still violate the GeoJSON contract. Assert the geometry type and the coordinate order. For a known query point, longitude should appear in element zero and latitude in element one.

Spatial boundaries deserve their own tests. A place at 999 meters should be included in a 1,000-meter search. A place at 1,001 meters should not. A place exactly at the boundary should behave consistently with the predicate you chose.

ST_DWithin includes features whose distance is less than or equal to the supplied threshold, so document that behavior and test it explicitly.

Unit tests are useful for request validation, but mocking the repository layer removes the most important part of this API: PostGIS itself. Keep a small integration-test database and run at least a few tests against the real extension.

That catches mistakes that mocks cannot: geography versus geometry behavior, SRID mismatches, spatial indexes, units, and changes to SQL functions. A location API is one of the cases where a cheap database integration test buys a lot of confidence.

Correctness is only half the story. A radius endpoint that scans every feature will work in development and become painful at production scale. Add a GiST index and inspect the query plan.

The exact plan depends on your data and PostgreSQL version, but you should see the spatial index participating in candidate filtering. Treat an accidental sequential scan on a large production table as a regression worth investigating.

For a real project, I would split the tests into two groups. Fast validation tests run on every commit. PostGIS integration tests run in CI with a temporary PostgreSQL/PostGIS service.

The CI gate should cover invalid coordinates, zero or negative radius values, known-distance fixtures, boundary behavior, GeoJSON output, and at least one query-plan or performance sanity check for larger datasets.

This is more work than asserting status_code == 200, but it tests the thing users actually care about: whether the API's answer is geographically true.

Location APIs fail in ways ordinary web tests are not designed to notice. The response can have the right schema, the database call can succeed, and every field can look reasonable while the location itself is wrong.

The fix is not a giant testing framework. Start with a few spatial invariants you can prove: known distances, valid coordinate ranges, correct GeoJSON order, deterministic boundary behavior, and real PostGIS integration tests. Those checks turn geography from an assumption into something your CI pipeline can verify.

#10532. Canva just laid off 1,200 people. But its severance package is earning praise

Design tech company Canva is doing some major restructuring: The move will impact about 1,200 employees, or roughly 22% of its staff. But the company’s also getting attention for how it’s treating the newly terminated employees. 

On Tuesday, CEO Melanie Perkins announced the news in a post on LinkedIn. She also shared a letter that laid out a generous severance package that’s being fawned over on social media.

The letter explained that all terminated employees would receive six months of salary,  regardless of location. The Sydney-based company also said it will remove the one-year vesting cliff for those who joined the company within the last year, which means even those who recently joined can walk away with shares in the company. 

They will also continue to receive healthcare, plus dedicated career support, resume help, coaching and interview preparation, plus one year of LinkedIn Premium. The company also launched a fund to provide $10,000 grants to those looking to start a company or project or their own. “Whether it’s starting a business or doing something meaningful for their local community, the fund is designed to help get those ideas off the ground,” Canva explained in the letter. 

The company is even allowing all terminated employees to keep their MacBook laptops.

“We’re making significant changes to how we’re organised, which sadly means saying goodbye to many exceptionally talented people who have helped build Canva into what it is today,” Perkins wrote in her LinkedIn post.

Perkins added that the company put in the time and effort to create “an opt-in alumni directory” for those who are being forced to leave the company, where former employees can learn about work opportunities. Perkins also included her email address and asked leaders with any work opportunities to reach out to her directly.

The CEO didn’t specify a reason for the layoffs in the note. But the news comes at a time in which the company is gearing up for a potential IPO following several years of spending on its suite of AI-powered products.

The CEO continued: “This is the hardest decision we’ve made in Canva’s history, and we know it will deeply impact many people and their loved ones. While we believe these changes are critical to help set Canva up for the future, Canva would not be the company it is today without their hard work, and we want to do everything we can to help set them up well for their next chapter.”

More often than not, when companies go through massive, major overhauls (like laying off nearly a quarter of their employees), the news is about how those employees may struggle to find employment, or how the company failed to support them. 

But Canva has seemed to take a more humane approach than we’re used to. In today’s era of forever layoffs, companies drop staff with decades of loyalty abruptly over a group Zoom call, and that’s it.

Commenters on the CEO’s post were quick to weigh in on how the company is showing other leaders how to gracefully handle layoffs. 

“Really impressive, empathetic, transparent, and generous way to communicate what was undoubtedly a very hard decision,” one LinkedIn commenter replied. “Especially with what this industry has seen over the past year, this is an example for other organizations on how to do a hard thing right.”

Another added, “Plenty of companies will do layoffs this year. Few will do them like this.” 

That’s likely the case, but with all of the positive attention surrounding Canva’s restructuring layoffs, it’s hard to imagine that it won’t inspire at least a few leaders to take note. Or at least, inspire more workers elsewhere to push for this in the future after being shown the door.

#10530. From Cameo To Lead Role: AI Takes Over Ransomware

Etay Maor is Vice President of Threat Intelligence for Cato Networks, a converged network and security cloud for the AI era.

​As much as 48% of breaches involve ransomware, and AI is making it more effective. While AI has certainly made malware smarter, it has also enabled unskilled actors to run attacks that were once the domain of highly trained threat actors.

AI has essentially democratized the ransomware attack vector.

Most ransomware today is available as ransomware-as-a-service (RaaS) kits. There is a core group that builds the malware and manages the leak site that publishes stolen data. Affiliates carry out the attack and pay the core group a share of the ransom they collect.

From the perspective of the affiliate, getting into the network is the first step, but the real work comes afterward. It involves figuring out the network structure, identifying the systems that are attack-worthy and ensuring they stay hidden long enough to deploy the encryptor that locks the victim’s files. This process takes days or even weeks of hands-on work. Ransomware negotiation is also a manual effort, typically involving an individual who might or might not have a real sense of what the data is actually worth.

Not every affiliate is a master at launching a successful ransomware attack. They work on a limited number of victims at a time. While defenders can pat themselves on the back for deflecting an attempted attack, many times, their defenses appear better than they actually were because the attack was conducted by amateurs.

Last year, the number of active ransomware groups rose 49%, according to IBM. Part of the reason is AI, which lets attackers automate processes that used to take skill and time. Affiliates see AI as a great leveler to fill in the missing know-how that can help accelerate attacks at scale.

This has led to AI showing up in ransomware in three distinct ways:

1. The Sales Pitch: Ransomware services are giving center stage to AI in their ads to woo affiliates. Some of the lofty claims made in these advertisements can’t be confirmed, but they do give us an indication of which way the wind is blowing. Affiliates want AI tools, and this isn’t just empty talk. A group handed its ransomware negotiations to an AI chatbot, which meant victims were pressured to pay around the clock instead of only when a human negotiator was available.

2. The Dependable Assistant: Ransomware threat actors recently used a widely available AI coding tool that enabled them to break into at least six organizations. Instead of doing each step manually, the AI did much of the work inside the network, including ranking databases by how much they would be worth in an extortion demand.

3. Inside The Product: Some newer RaaS kits go a step further. Their control panels are run by an LLM, which sellers say can perform multiple actions including scanning infected machines, keeping track of several victims simultaneously and writing ransom notes. Of course, buyers haven’t confirmed any of these features yet, but if this turnkey kit works as advertised, an affiliate doesn’t need much experience to manage it.

The kind of work that originally took days can now be done in hours. Security teams don’t have much time to spot an attack before it can cause extensive damage.

AI tools can also run several attacks at once and reply to victims in their own language at any hour. A typical setup these days involves AI handling the first contact, followed by a human joining the party in cases of large ransomware amounts.

Finally, RaaS services are cheap, with some selling for as low as $40 per month. The cost of launching AI attacks at scale is not prohibitive anymore.

A two-pronged approach will help security teams defend against these growing threats.

First, look for signs of AI in attacks. AI-written attack code often gives itself away, with long step-by-step comments and plain-English notes left inside scripts. Another warning sign is a server program that has no reason to use AI suddenly connecting to an AI service. Such traffic should be investigated.

Second, improve your ability to recover. Many AI tools used for ransomware focus on stopping victims from restoring their data. This is why you must:

• Keep backups offline, in a form that can’t be changed or deleted.

• Test restores regularly, not just backups.

• Alert immediately when anyone tries to delete backups.

AI has turned ransomware from a specialized craft into a mass-market commodity. By filling in the missing skills for amateurs, AI lets them strike with the scale and precision of elite attackers, shrinking defensive response windows from days to hours.

Because these automated attacks move too fast for traditional prevention to keep up, protecting the business comes down to proactive threat hunting and regularly tested recovery plans. We can’t just focus on building taller walls; survival hinges on how fast teams can bounce back when a strike happens.​​

#10525. 7 Checks Developers Should Make So AI Search Can Read Their Site

Have 30-200 Employees? Make $50k-$500k selling your data for AI Training.

Have 30-200 Employees? Make $50k-$500k selling your data for AI Training.

Stay up to date with AI tools, model releases, and developer workflows that matter.

Search results now include AI-written answers that cite pages, and people increasingly ask chat tools for recommendations instead of scrolling a list of links. For developers, this does not mean learning a new discipline. It means making sure the basics are in place so that crawlers and answer engines can reach, read and quote your pages.

Most problems are plain engineering mistakes: a blocked crawler, a page that renders nothing without JavaScript, or markup that disagrees with the visible text. This article covers seven checks, including one script you can run against your own robots.txt.

AI features in search do not need a special file or a special format. Google's documentation on AI features and your website states that a page needs to be indexed and eligible to appear in Search with a snippet, and that there are no additional technical requirements. It also says there is no need for new AI-specific files or special schema.org markup.

So start with the fundamentals. Check for accidental noindex tags after a deploy, confirm important pages return a 200 status, and make sure staging settings never reach production.

Answer engines read text. If your key information lives in images, canvas elements or content that only appears after a client-side script runs, a crawler may never see it. View the page source and the rendered HTML, and compare them. Product names, prices, definitions and steps should be present as real text.

Structured data helps systems understand a page, but only if it agrees with what visitors see. SitePoint's guide to JSON-LD for developers shows how to build markup that search and AI systems can parse. Generate it from the same data that renders the page, and validate it after every template change. Markup that contradicts the visible text is worse than no markup.

Your robots.txt decides which crawlers may fetch your pages. Some sites block AI crawlers deliberately, and others block them by accident through a broad rule. SitePoint's technical guide to working with a marketing agency lists robots.txt decisions about which crawlers may access the site among the checks developers should own.

This small function reads a robots.txt string and reports which common AI-related crawlers are blocked from the whole site:

Run it against your live robots.txt. If a crawler appears in the list and you did not intend that, fix the rule. Note that blocking a crawler is a legitimate choice. The goal is that it is a decision and not an accident.

Developers can check access and markup, but judging how a brand shows up in AI answers often needs someone who tracks that area full time. An AI search consultant such as Austin Heaton works on answer engine optimization.

Traffic from AI features in Google Search is included in the Search Console Performance report under the Web search type. Set up that report, tag your own campaigns with consistent UTM parameters, and watch referral traffic from chat tools in your analytics. You cannot control the answers, but you can see whether clicks arrive.

Most visibility problems appear after a deployment: a template change drops the structured data, a new rule blocks a crawler, or a redesign hides text behind a script. Add a small post-deploy test for the checks above. A failing robots.txt check or a missing JSON-LD block should stop the release before a crawler finds the problem.

Do I need an llms.txt file or special markup for AI search? Google's documentation says no new AI-specific files or special structured data are needed for its AI features. Standard indexing and crawling requirements apply.

Should I block AI crawlers? That depends on your goals. Blocking is a legitimate choice, but make it deliberately and review it regularly.

Where do I see AI search traffic? For Google, AI feature traffic is counted in the Search Console Performance report under the Web search type. Other tools show up as referrals in your analytics.

Making a site readable to AI search is mostly ordinary engineering: keep pages indexable, put key content in text, keep structured data consistent, decide crawler access on purpose, measure what you can and retest after every release. The robots.txt check above is small, but it catches one of the most common accidental blocks before it costs you visibility.
